news.title: Biden’s ‘startlingly dull’ memoir flops
news.text:
Former US President Joe Biden’s memoir sold just 21,000 copies in its first week despite the author reportedly receiving a $10 million advance, multiple media outlets reported on Friday, citing market research firm Circana.

Critics described the 480-page book, Promise Me, America, released on November 17, as offering few new insights and faulted the 84-year-old Democrat for failing to meaningfully reflect on his mistakes during his presidency from 2021 to 2025.

“Honestly, it’s like who the f**k cares anymore about Joe Biden,” a former Biden aide told the New York Post when asked about the poor sales.

According to AP, Barack Obama’s A Promised Land sold more than 1 million copies in its first week in 2020, while Bill Clinton’s My Life sold more than 1 million copies within two weeks in 2004.

Biden has done little to promote the book. The former president was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer in May 2025.

Amy Davidson Sorkin of The New Yorker described Biden’s book as “startlingly dull,” writing that “much of it has the feel of something written by a committee – and a committee of which Biden himself need not have been a member.”

Writing for The New York Times, Jennifer Szalai argued that Biden was “awkward and defensive” when addressing two controversial aspects of his presidency: his handling of Israel’s war in Gaza and his decision to run for a second term.

Having served as Obama’s vice president for eight years, Biden was elected president in 2020. Despite initially portraying himself as a transitional leader and mounting concerns about his age and health, he sought reelection before abruptly withdrawing from the race less than four months before the vote. He endorsed Vice President Kamala Harris, who went on to lose to Donald Trump.
news.summary:
Joe Biden’s memoir sold just 21,000 copies in its first week, with critics panning the book as dull and defensive

news.title: The Man Who Made Kamala Harris Says She Shouldn't Run In 2028
news.text:
The 2028 Democratic presidential nomination race has no clear front-runner, with former VP Kamala Harris currently topping the RealClearPolitics national average at 16.5%. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) is at 15%, with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and former Transportation Sec. Pete Buttigieg both at 14%.

Harris started strong in 2028 polling after losing to Trump in 2024, but her numbers are slipping as other Democrats are gaining traction. Ossoff, in particular, has surged from single digits to 15-18% since the midterms. The message Democrat voters are sending is clear: Harris's grip is weak.

Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA), long seen as plotting a 2028 presidential run, has slipped to fifth at 11%. Harris's numbers are even worse in key states. In New Hampshire, she sinks to 6% while Buttigieg takes the lead.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Nov. 12 asked Democratic voters which potential candidates would make an excellent nominee. Ossoff and Buttigieg led at 29% each, with Harris and Newsom tied at 23%.

Willie Brown (D-CA), the 92-year-old former San Francisco mayor who spent decades as one of California's most powerful political figures, began dating Harris in the mid-1990s, when she was a 29-year-old prosecutor and he was 60. As speaker of the California Assembly, Brown appointed her to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board and the California Medical Assistance Commission. He has since said he helped her win the 2003 race for San Francisco district attorney, including in a 2019 San Francisco Chronicle column.

Over lunch with The Red Letter at John's Grill in San Francisco on Saturday, Nov. 21, Brown said he doesn't want Harris running for president again in 2028.

"I'm sorry that she even thinks about running for president," Brown said. "I don't want her to run."

Brown also told the outlet, "She was clearly very hurt."

Brown has questioned whether Harris has the speaking style and presence to win over voters and command a room, saying she has no "Baptist preacher flavor in her soul." He noted that she already reached the highest elected office any American woman has held, serving four years as vice president under Joe Biden.

Brown suggested she consider roles outside electoral politics, such as leading a major institution or working in media. He has also said he was surprised she didn't run for governor of California, a move he believes could have strengthened her national standing.

Polls suggested that had she run for governor of California, she would have been the frontrunner.

Brown also launched Gavin Newsom's career. He appointed Newsom to San Francisco's Parking and Traffic Commission, helped him win a seat on the city's Board of Supervisors, and backed his successful 2003 run for mayor. At a 2024 ceremony inducting Brown into the California Hall of Fame, Newsom credited his former patron.

"I'm standing here because of Willie Brown," Newsom said.

In June 2026, Brown told ABC News that Newsom held an edge over Harris because he was not the "most recent loser."

"When you embrace somebody for the job, you really want to embrace a winner," Brown said. "And Newsom would be what you would have to say at the moment is a winner."

Newsom, however, has tied his own plans to Harris's decision. During a CNN interview with Jake Tapper that aired in September, Newsom said he would stay out of the race if she entered it.

"I don't know if she runs, but we'll see," Newsom said. "I wouldn't run if she ran."

Tapper asked, "If she runs, you will not?"

"Of course not. Why would I? I wouldn't do that to her. I wouldn't do it to me. I wouldn't do that to you. I wouldn't waste everyone's time. Who needs that?" Newsom said.

He described a primary between the two Californians as a "gift from God for everybody else. They'd enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good." Newsom said that the overlap between their political bases would make it impossible for either to succeed in a primary.

"I know her base of supporters, I know her friends, the Venn diagram on that is just pure crossover," Newsom said. "I wouldn't do that to people."

Newsom tells @jaketapper he won't run in 2028 if Kamala Harris runs. pic.twitter.com/auDjNdBlyr— Alex Thompson (@AlexThomp) September 14, 2026

Harris has not said publicly whether she will run again in 2028.

Kamala Harris's Thanksgiving photo with husband Doug Emhoff became a magnet for online trolls after her former flame, Willie Brown, publicly urged the former vice president to stay out of the 2028 White House race, RadarOnline.com can reveal. 

Harris, 62, famously dated Brown, 92, a California political kingpin 30 years her senior, in the mid-1990s. Their decades-old romance was dragged back into the spotlight after the former San Francisco mayor and political heavyweight made his latest stinging remarks about her presidential ambitions.Kamala Harris Shares Thanksgiving Post Featuring Husband Doug EmhoffHarris and Emhoff, 62, flashed beaming smiles in their kitchen as the former veep proudly held up what looked like a freshly whipped-up casserole in the Thanksgiving Day photo she shared on Facebook on Thursday, November 26.

"From our family to yours, happy Thanksgiving," she captioned the appetizing snapshot. 

While some in the comments debated whether the casserole was mac and cheese or cornbread, others used the occasion to take shots at her May-December romance with Brown, which launched her political ambitions.'Was Willie Brown Invited Over' for Thanksgiving?"Was Willie Brown invited over?" one person asked in the comments on Harris' Thanksgiving post, while a second wondered, "Where's Willie?" about her ex.

A fifth joked about their past relationship and her Thanksgiving dish, "Willie gave you a good stuffing."Kamala Harris' Ex Willie Brown Doesn't Want Her to Run for President in 2028Brown made headlines after journalist Tara Palmeri published his remarks in her The Red Letter Substack on November 23. "I'm sorry that she even thinks about running for president. I don't want her to run. She clearly was very hurt," Brown shared.

In a San Francisco Chronicle op-ed titled "Sure, I dated Kamala Harris. So what?" Brown wrote: "Yes, we dated. It was more than 20 years ago. Yes, I may have influenced her career by appointing her to two state commissions when I was Assembly Speaker."

"And I certainly helped with her first race for district attorney in San Francisco," he continued, referring to Harris' successful 2003 campaign.

Harris used her victory in San Francisco as a springboard to higher office, winning the California attorney general's race in 2010 before securing a U.S. Senate seat in 2016. Her political rise culminated in 2020 when Joe Biden tapped her as his running mate, paving the way for her to become the nation's first female vice president.

However, Brown was quick to point out that Harris was hardly the only California Bay Area politician whose career he helped advance, noting that he had also championed plenty of rising political stars he never dated.

"I have also helped the careers of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Gov. Gavin Newsom, Sen. Dianne Feinstein and a host of other politicians," he added.
news.summary: Kamala Harris' Thanksgiving photo with Doug Emhoff sparked trolling after her ex, Willie Brown, urged her to stay out of the 2028 race.

news.title: All the times The Simpsons made eerily accurate predictions about California
news.text:
Life often imitates art.

And The Simpsons has long been lauded for the eerie accuracy with which it has predicted the future.

Donald Trump’s presidency, Richard Branson’s launch into space and Kamala Harris‘ purple pantsuit are all among the animated sequences that came true years later.

But what has the long-running series, which first aired in 1989, correctly anticipated for California?

The California Post has taken a look at all the times it has tackled topics in the state that then seemingly came true.

LA Wildfires

Back in January 2025, Los Angeles was ravaged by the most destructive fires in California’s history.

More than 400 people were killed, entire neighborhoods were destroyed and thousands of families were displaced with the two biggest blazes being in the Palisades and Eaton.

The cause of the Palisades Fire was later identified as being deliberate arson — with an eerie echo to an episode of The Simpsons from 2007.

In Season 18, Episode 12, titled Little Big Girl, one of Bart’s pranks ends up sparking a fire that quickly spirals out of control.

Springfield is then left battling a devastating wildfire that threatens the town and its residents. Dozens of properties are destroyed despite valiant efforts from firefighters to contain the inferno.

“Coincidence or yet another unsettling prediction?” one TikTok creator asked at the time of the LA wildfires.

Power Blackout

Earlier this month, between November 16 and 23, California battled a series of power outages, with Buena Park in Orange County particularly impacted.

The outage coincided with the avalanche of technological failures felt nationwide that affected aviation, email, banks and online retailers.

But did The Simpsons give advanced warning?

In 2023, in Series 35, Episode 7, titled It’s a Blunderful Life, documented a massive outage in Springfield right before Thanksgiving.

The story is told by Lisa, decades into the future, as she recounts what happened during “the great blackout that almost destroyed the town.”

Rise of Silicon Valley

The Simpsons’ 1996 episode titled “You Only Move Twice” is widely cited for foreshadowing modern Silicon Valley culture.

In Season 8, Episode 2, which aired long before the rise of tech titans in the San Francisco hotspot, Homer moves out of Springfield to accept a job at the Globex Corporation in Cypress Creek.

The show sees employees enjoying lavish perks and a relaxed workplace culture, mirroring modern tech campuses that prioritize comfort and loyalty.

Globex CEO Hank Scorpio is branded as a friendly supervillain who acts warm, generous and supportive toward Homer while secretly pursuing global domination.

“It’s crazy that all this was predicted 20 years ago before Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg turned the world upside-down,” one conspiracy theorist said in a YouTube analysis.

Creation of Smart Watches

Speaking of tech giants, Silicon Valley-based Apple unveiled its first smartwatch in September 2014.

But back in 1995, The Simpsons’ episode titled Lisa’s Wedding — from Season 6, Episode 19 — sees a fortuneteller giving the eight-year-old a glimpse of the future.

She takes Homer and Marge’s youngest kid forward to the year 2010 where Lisa’s fiance holds his wristwatch up to his mouth to make a call.

It was not until several years later that smartwatches and face-to-face mobile video became standard.

Disney-Fox Consolidation

In 2017, news broke about California-based Disney’s $52.4 billion purchase of 21st Century Fox assets.

But it seems that the move was predicted back in The Simpsons’ 1998 episode titled When You Dish Upon a Star.

In it, airing Season 10, Episode 5, director Ron Howard arrives at the Fox Lot in Los Angeles to pitch an idea to film producer Brian Grazer.

The episode includes a brief visual gag showing a 20th Century Fox studio sign with the words “A Division of Walt Disney Co.” underneath.

news.title: Chuck Schumer's Approval Rating Compared to Trump Amid Van Hollen Challenge
news.text: For months, critics of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer have repeated a pointed talking point—The New York Democrat is less popular than President Donald Trump. Mark Ruffalo echoed the claim in a video this week urging fans to call their senators. "Chuck Schumer has a lower public approval rating than Trump. Read that again," the actor said. Polling data largely supports the assertion. Fewer Americans hold a favorable view of Schumer than of Trump in nearly every recent national survey. However, because roughly a quarter of the country says it has never heard of the senator, his negative numbers remain lower than the president's—leaving Schumer with a slightly better net rating in at least one major poll. The comparison carries heightened stakes as Schumer faces the first contested race for Senate Democratic leader since 1994. Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging him for the majority leader post after Democrats reclaimed control of the chamber in the November 3 midterm elections. Senate Democrats will choose their leader by secret ballot on December 1. Newsweek reached out to Schumer's and Van Hollen's campaign teams for comment via email. What the Polls Show A Pew Research Center survey of more than 10,000 adults, conducted November 9-15, evaluated both men using identical phrasing. It found 22 percent of respondents viewed Schumer favorably and 49 percent unfavorably, while 26 percent had never heard of him. Trump drew a 33 percent favorable rating and a 64 percent unfavorable rating. While Schumer trailed Trump by 11 percentage points in positive views, his net rating of -27 edged out Trump's -31. Other recent surveys show a similar gap in positive sentiment, though pollsters often measure Trump’s job approval alongside Schumer’s personal favorability: Trump's own numbers have slid since Republicans lost control of both congressional chambers, dropping to an all-time low of 32 percent in both a November 9-11 Economist/YouGov poll and a Reuters/Ipsos survey. Still, Schumer's standing within his own party remains notably softer than Trump's among Republicans. Pew found 67 percent of Republicans viewed Trump favorably, whereas Democrats leaned against Schumer, with 33 percent viewing him favorably and 40 percent unfavorably. Two Years of Frustration Schumer's slide with his own voters traces back to March 2025. He and nine other Senate Democrats voted to advance a Republican-written funding bill and avoid a shutdown, a move many on the left saw as giving away the party's only leverage over Trump. The progressive group Indivisible called on him to step aside the next day, after 91 percent of its group leaders nationwide voted for the demand. Co-executive director Ezra Levin said Schumer "led the charge to wave the white flag of surrender." House Democrats reportedly urged New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to think about a primary challenge, and Schumer canceled stops on his book tour amid protests. Comedian Jon Stewart spent much of a Daily Show opening segment on the vote, calling it a "total capitulation" to Trump and Republicans. By April 2025, a CNN survey had Schumer at 17 percent favorable, his worst showing in CNN polling since 2017. CNN's Manu Raju asked him about it at a press conference, minutes after Schumer had been touting Trump's poor approval numbers. "Polls come and go," Schumer said. Frustration mounted again in the fall of 2025 when a 43-day government shutdown ended after eight Senate Democrats broke ranks to vote with Republicans. Although Schumer voted against the measure, critics faulted his leadership strategy, and more than 50 progressive organizations called for him to relinquish his post. This year, the pushback reached the ballot. Several Democratic Senate primary winners, including Juliana Stratton in Illinois, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, ran while refusing to back Schumer. Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin said the party needed "significant new leadership." A Politico poll in June found 47 percent of likely Democratic voters wanted Schumer to step down from leadership, compared with 28 percent who wanted him to stay. A Siena College poll of New York voters late last year showed his worst approval rating at 32 percent at home in 21 years of surveys. How the Van Hollen Challenge Emerged Progressive groups first floated Van Hollen as a potential successor in November 2025, though Axios reported at the time that he was not seeking the role. El-Sayed urged him to run as early as April during Michigan's Senate primary. Following the midterms, Van Hollen said Democrats should not hand Schumer a "coronation" and spent roughly a week consulting colleagues before launching his bid on November 12. "To deliver, we need new leadership," he wrote on X. "This isn't about any one person." Schumer then responded without naming his challenger. "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," he wrote, citing the party's 55-seat majority. An Economist/YouGov poll of 1,623 U.S. adult citizens, conducted November 20-23, found 40 percent of Democrats preferred Van Hollen to lead the Senate caucus, compared with 19 percent for Schumer. Among 2024 voters who backed then-Vice President Kamala Harris, Van Hollen led 48 percent to 18 percent. Van Hollen has noted that Schumer and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) backed the primary opponents of El-Sayed and Flanagan, both of whom won anyway. He has also accused party leadership of siding with the cryptocurrency industry and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC)—highlighting U.S. policy toward Israel as a major policy divide between the two senators. In an ABC News interview earlier this month, Van Hollen alleged Schumer's allies were attempting to "instill fear" in senators considering defection. Van Hollen's public backers include independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, Oregon Senator Jeff Merkley and Slotkin, along with Senators-elect El-Sayed and Flanagan. Outside the chamber, MoveOn, Indivisible, Our Revolution, the Working Families Party, National Nurses United and the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Worker, shave lined up behind him. About 35 celebrities and donors, among them Jane Fonda and Robert De Niro, signed a letter supporting him, and online petitions to replace Schumer passed 100,000 signatures. Wisconsin Senator Tammy Baldwin, Nevada Senator Jacky Rosen and Maine Senator Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, say the party gained seats under Schumer. King asked why anyone would fire a manager who just won the World Series. "Chuck delivered an amazing win," Virginia Senator Tim Kaine said, though he added he is open to other candidates. Trump has also taken shots at Schumer as the race heats up. “It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,” the president wrote on Truth Social earlier this week. What Is Expected on December 1 Assuming every caucus member participates and a simple majority is required; a candidate would need 28 votes in a 55-member caucus or 29 in a 56-member caucus to win the leadership race. Because the vote is conducted by secret ballot, public endorsements are nonbinding. As of Sunday, at least 16 Democrats had publicly endorsed Schumer, compared with six for Van Hollen. An unofficial tally by Drop Site News counted 16 senators committed to or leaning toward Schumer and nine toward Van Hollen, while a Washington Post tally found 30 of the 55 senators had made no public commitment. Four incoming Democrats—Adam Hamilton, Troy Jackson, Chris Pappas and Stratton—have said they will not support Schumer but have not endorsed Van Hollen. Van Hollen said on November 22 that he had support from "north of 15" senators, while Schumer's allies project he will clear 40 votes. As of Thursday, the prediction market Kalshi gave Schumer a 91 percent chance of keeping the job and Polymarket put it at 92 percent. Van Hollen, meanwhile, has acknowledged he is the underdog, telling The Hill this week it is still a "wide-open race." Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Jason Lemon and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: Schumer trails President Trump in popularity and recent polling shows his own voters prefer Senator Chris Van Hollen as leader.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: Liberal media and fans want Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker to fail because he's a Catholic conservative
news.text: Few NFL players have drawn as much personal disdain from the political left as Kansas City Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker. The outspoken Catholic conservative has become a target for liberal sports fans and media personalities since delivering his 2024 commencement address at Benedictine College. His public support for Donald Trump, the Republican Party, campaigning with Senator Josh Hawley, and advocacy for traditional family values have only intensified that criticism. Butker has been branded a misogynist for expressing the belief that motherhood is more fulfilling for women than climbing the corporate ladder. A stance that clearly aligns with his Catholic faith and those that attend Benedictine College, a Catholic college, which he was speaking too directly. Since then, as we have seen from some of his most vocal critics, watching Butker miss field goals over the years, especially this season, appears to provide a sense of political vindication. Unfortunately, the three-time Super Bowl champion has given those critics plenty of ammunition this season from media and fans. WIFE OF PATRICK MAHOMES UNLEASHES FIRE AND FURY TOWARDS REFS AFTER BOTCHED CALL IN BUFFALO Mina Kimes, Nick Wright, and Other Media and Fans Have Butker Living Rent Free Many media members are still taking shots at Butker for his comments in the commencement speech years later. On Pablo Torre's Thanksgiving episode, he invited ESPN's Mina Kimes and the clip shared on X had a caption that said, "Harrison Butker may not like our Thanksgiving episode." The clip featured a male cook preparing some Thanksgiving dishes. Mina Kimes, still clearly triggered by Butker said, "How triggered do you think Harrison Butker would be if he turned this on and saw a bunch of men cooking for me?" Good grief. MINA KIMES CRACKS HARRISON BUTKER JOKE ABOUT MEN IN THE KITCHEN WITH CALLBACK TO KICKER'S COMMENCEMENT SPEECH After the Chiefs worst game of the season on Sunday Night Football against the Seattle Seahawks, also being Butker's worst game of the season, going 1-for-3 on field goals, Nick Wright took a political shot at Butker. "He started splitting his time between football and activism, and he hasn't been quite as good. That is just the timeline of it," Wright said. There's clearly a political bias here and even making this topic political is unprofessional, in my opinion. Also, Butker didn't immediately regress after becoming more politically outspoken. In fact, he converted every field goal and extra point he attempted between campaigning with Senator Josh Hawley during the Chiefs bye week in 2024 and suffering his knee injury. Maybe Wright should've spoken about how the knee injury and becoming the NFL's highest paid kicker could have effected Butker's performance. On Thanksgiving fans took plenty of shots at Butker after missing a crucial 46-yard field goal with the game tied against the Buffalo Bills. Denver news anchor Kyle Clark posted on X, "Butker. Wide right. Happy Thanksgiving, America." He later responded to a comment about rooting for and against players based on political party affiliation, Clark said, "Hi anonymous friend. Happy to clear this up for you. Whether my wife and my daughters should be able to have a job is not politics. It’s human rights. Have a Happy Thanksgiving!" Again, a false retelling of what Butker said and believes. Former Minnesota Star Tribune journalist Jim Souhan said, "Someone said that Butker’s pronouns are Miss/Misses and I’ll never forget it." Editor-in Chief at radically liberal news outlet Meidas Touch, Ron Filipkowski took a shot as well by sharing a photo of Butker with President Trump on top of a post from an Associated Press reporter that stated, "Harrison Butker is tied with Trey Smack for most missed kicks this season with 9 (8 FGs, 1 PAT) and his 24 missed kicks (17 FGs, 7 PATs) since start of 2024 are most in NFL." Obviously, when Butker misses to the right, the jokes write themselves, so those don't bother me. It's the low-hanging fruit that is easy to pick. What we do need to discuss is how bad Butker has been statistically can be somewhat misleading. Butker's Struggles Are Real, But The Numbers Need Context In August 2024, 86 days after his controversial commencement speech at Benedictine College, the Kansas City Chiefs rewarded Butker with a four-year, $25.6 million contract extension, making him the highest-paid kicker in NFL history at the time. Whether you're right, left, or center, you could agree at that time, Butker deserved this. The Chiefs clearly did not care that liberals were calling for Butker to be cut from the team for his comments on traditional roles within the household. Butker was coming off a 2023 campaign in which he converted 33 of his 35 field goal attempts and made every extra point. He also drilled a Super Bowl-record 57-yard field goal against the San Francisco 49ers. He was arguably the Super Bowl MVP for much of the game. Unfortunately, his field goal percentage has declined every season since signing that lucrative extension. Butker currently owns the worst field goal percentage among NFL kickers with at least 15 attempts this season. However, a closer examination of his numbers reveals that his struggles are overwhelmingly concentrated in one area: long-distance field goals. According to NFL.com, Butker has converted just two of his eight attempts from 50-plus yards this season (25%). From inside 50 yards, he's 13-of-15 (86.7%), including a perfect 7-of-7 from inside 40 yards. It's particulary shocking to see how bad he's been from distance because he hit a 69-yard field goal in preseason, which most likely would've been good from almost 80 yards. HARRISON BUTKER'S 69-YARD FIELD GOAL DEMONSTRATES THE NFL'S LATEST BIG SCORING CONTROVERSY Butker isn't the only highly compensated kicker struggling from deep, either. Dallas Cowboys kicker Brandon Aubrey, who surpassed Butker as the highest-paid kicker in NFL history after signing a four-year, $28 million extension in April, is also experiencing the worst season of his career. Aubrey has converted just six of his 11 attempts from 50-plus yards (54.5%) and is shooting a career-low 77.8% overall. He also missed a 40-yard field goal on Thanksgiving in Dallas' one-point loss to Philadelphia. That kick has been heavily debated online, with former Colts punter and placeholder Pat McAfee giving Aubrey grace because the laces were facing toward Aubrey. Speaking about Aubrey's stats are not an excuse for Butker's poor performance, but it does provide some much-needed perspective. Clearly his struggles are not as scrutinized as Butker's, though he's paid more. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Best Revenge Is Success There is a difference between rooting for someone to fail because of their religious and political beliefs and legitimately criticizing their professional performance. Butker deserves the latter right now. If you know me at all, I am not a LeBron James fan. Yes, his politics come into play in my dislike of him, but claiming poor play is because of campaigning for Hilary Clinton or Kamala Harris by me would hopefully cause many to scold me for refusing to provide proper sports analysis and instead, going for a political cheapshot. In all honestly, I'd love nothing more than to see Butker return to being one of the most reliable kickers in football. But defending his right to express his Catholic faith and conservative values doesn't require defending his inability to consistently put a football through the uprights, especially from long distance. The Chiefs are paying him elite money to deliver elite results, particularly in high-pressure situations with championship aspirations on the line. He has no one to blame but himself. He needs to be better. Butker doesn't need to apologize for his faith, his political affiliations or his appreciation for traditional family values. He just needs to start making kicks again. Until he does that, his critics, in and out of the media, will continue to tee off on who they consider to be their political enemy.
news.summary: Harrison Butker's critics, including Mina Kimes and Nick Wright, claim his activism has hurt his play, but his stats tell a more complicated story.
news.author: Jon Root

news.title: GOP Senator Reveals Tragic Twist After Husband’s Death
news.text:
But the office of the Nebraska senator issued a second statement on Friday via X, saying “Bruce chose to end his life.”

“The family is deeply grateful for the recent outpouring of sympathy for their loss, and asks for understanding in this time of mourning,” the statement continued. “There will be no further comment and no other details will be provided.”

Bruce, 75, was a cattle rancher from Lincoln, Nebraska, who drew online criticism for seemingly refusing to shake then-Vice President Kamala Harris’ hand during the swearing-in of his wife to her third term in Congress.

Harris administered the oath with Bruce holding the Bible for his wife to place her hand on. 

Harris then shook Sen. Fischer’s hand and extended the offer to Bruce. He told Harris, “Thank you,” but didn’t shake her hand.

Defenders said he was holding a Bible in one hand and a cane in the other. But some say Bruce kept his free hand in his pocket, and Doug Emhoff, Harris’ husband, later rebuked him in person.

The Fischers never publicly explained the interaction.

At a White House tea in 2025 ahead of Trump’s inauguration, Bruce tried to shake Emhoff’s hand, and Emhoff declined with, “Why would you try to shake my hand when you wouldn’t shake my wife’s hand?” According to CNN, Bruce apologized.

The couple met as students at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, according to the Lincoln Journal Star, and married in 1972. They had been married 54 years and have three sons and six grandchildren.

Sen. Fischer’s initial statement announcing his death described him as her “beloved husband,” her “partner in life,” her “greatest source of strength,” and the “heart” of their family.

“His kindness, integrity, and quiet strength left a lasting impression on all who knew him,” Sen. Fischer, also 75, wrote.

It didn’t mention a cause of death, but it said he passed away “peacefully” while doing “what he loved most”—spending time outdoors.

Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee and Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen offered their condolences via X.

Lee wrote, “This is truly heartbreaking,” with Pillen saying, “Suzanne and I are keeping Sen. Fischer and her family in our thoughts.

We share our prayers as she deals with this great personal loss.”

The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is a hotline for individuals in crisis or for those looking to help someone else. To speak with a trained listener, call 988.
news.summary:
Nikos Frazier / Getty ImagesSen. Deb Fischer office has revealed that her husband, Bruce Fischer, was found to have died by suicide.

The initial statement, issued Monday, said he died “peacefully” on Sunday after spending time outdoors.

But the office of the Nebraska senator issued a second statement on Friday via X, saying “Bruce chose to end his life.”

news.title: Donald Trump Suffers Legal Blow After It's Discovered 'The View' Dropped Political Guests and Pulled On-Air Clips Amid Fears of Retaliation
news.text:
President Donald Trump's administration has suffered a legal setback after a federal judge intervened in a battle over ABC's broadcast licenses, as the network revealed it scrapped political guests and withheld footage from The View amid fears of government retaliation, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

According to court documents obtained by Radar, U.S. District Judge Loren L. AliKhan issued a 45-page ruling on November 25, denying the FCC's request to dismiss a lawsuit brought by ABC, Disney, and eight television stations.'The View' Under Federal InvestigationThe judge also granted part of the broadcasters' request for a preliminary injunction, temporarily blocking the FCC's early license renewal proceedings.

ABC and Disney accused the agency of using its regulatory powers to punish the network for broadcasting content critical of Trump and the Republican Party.

The FCC launched an investigation into The View in February 2026 following a U.S. Senate candidate's appearance, questioning whether the show violated federal rules requiring equal airtime opportunities for qualified political candidates.Co-Hosts' Political Donations Under ScrutinyDespite receiving an exemption from those requirements in 2002, ABC began evaluating whether political guests' appearances could jeopardize its broadcast licenses.

According to the filing, "no candidate for public office has appeared on The View" since the investigation began, and the network passed on several potential political bookings. ABC also acknowledged withholding clips it otherwise would have aired during the show's popular Hot Topics segment and opening sequence.

In July, the FCC demanded two years' worth of internal communications concerning political candidates, along with political donation records involving the show's staff and co-hosts.

The agency also requested information about employees' and co-hosts' political donations.Trump Calls for ABC's Licenses to Be RevokedSimilar demands extended to Good Morning America, This Week with George Stephanopoulos, and ABC World News Tonight with David Muir. The court documents also highlighted the White House's "Media Offenders" webpage, which featured The View co-hosts Whoopi Goldberg, Joy Behar and Ana Navarro.

Goldberg faced criticism over Trump's White House ballroom, while Behar was singled out for remarks about the president and his supporters.

The ruling detailed Trump's repeated calls for ABC to lose its broadcasting licenses, dating back to the September 2024 presidential debate against then-Vice President Kamala Harris. In August 2025, Trump accused ABC and NBC of unfairly covering Republicans, declaring their licenses should be revoked.Judge Warns FCC Against RetaliationThe documents also referenced a White House spokesperson who branded one of The View's co-hosts "an irrelevant loser" and suggested the program could be pulled off the air.

The FCC ordered eight ABC stations to submit early license renewal applications in April 2026, although none were due until at least 2028. The agency cited an ongoing investigation into Disney's employment practices.

AliKhan found ABC and Disney had demonstrated they were likely to succeed on their First Amendment retaliation claim. "This is not a close case," the judge wrote while weighing the public interest in granting the injunction.

She added: "Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech." The ruling does not prevent the FCC from pursuing other lawful investigations into the network.

The lawsuit remains ongoing.
news.summary: Donald Trump suffered a legal setback as ABC revealed 'The View' dropped political guests and withheld on-air clips amid fears of retaliation.

news.title: GOP Senator Deb Fischer’s Late Husband Died By Suicide
news.text:
Republican Nebraska Sen. Deb Fischer’s spokesperson announced Friday that her late husband died by suicide. 

Fischer’s family initially believed that her late husband, Bruce, died peacefully at their home on Sunday at the age of 75, but further investigation found that he took his life, a spokesperson for Fischer announced on X. The Nebraska senator first announced her husband’s passing in a Monday statement. 

“There has been a sad update in the death of Senator Fischer’s husband, Bruce,” Fischer’s spokesperson said. “Initially, it was believed that Bruce passed peacefully at home. Upon further investigation, it was learned that Bruce chose to end his life. The family is deeply grateful for the recent outpouring of sympathy for their loss, and asks for understanding in this time of mourning. There will be no further comment and no other details will be provided.” (RELATED: Republican Nebraska Sen. Deb Fischer Attends Elite DC Party Hosted By Major Gay Dating App)

A spokesperson for the office of Senator Deb Fischer issued the following statement today: There has been a sad update in the death of Senator Fischer’s husband, Bruce. Initially, it was believed that Bruce passed peacefully at home. Upon further investigation, it was learned that Bruce chose to end his life. The family is deeply grateful for the recent outpouring of sympathy for their loss, and asks for understanding in this time of mourning. There will be no further comment and no other details will be provided.— Senator Deb Fischer (@SenatorFischer) November 27, 2026

Fischer and her late husband were married for 54 years. In her initially announcement, Fischer referred to Bruce as her “partner in life, my greatest source of strength, and the heart of our family.

“Our family is heartbroken by his passing, but we find comfort in the life we shared with him,” Fischer said in a Monday statement. “I will cherish the decades we spent building a family in the Nebraska Sandhills. Above all, Bruce was a loving husband, a devoted father and grandfather, a man of faith and a rancher. We sincerely appreciate the prayers, kindness, and support extended to our family during this difficult time.” 

The Nebraska senator met Bruce at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, according to her Senate profile. They married in 1972 and raised their three sons on their family ranch in Valentine, Nebraska. 

Republican Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen and Republican Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts expressed their condolences over the passing of Fischer’s husband. 

“Suzanne and I are keeping Sen. Fischer and her family in our thoughts. We share our prayers as she deals with this great personal loss,” Pillen said in a Monday statement. 

“Bruce left his mark on this world through his love for family, his faith, and his ranch,” Ricketts said. “Susanne and I send our deepest condolences to Deb, the entire Fischer family, and all their loved ones during this difficult time. The Fischer family is in our prayers.”

Footage from January 2025 showed Bruce appearing to decline to shake hands with then-Vice President Kamala Harris as his wife was being sworn in.

news.title: Trump keeps Vance, Rubio guessing on 2028 endorsement while also praising Hegseth for doing a ’great job
news.text:
WASHINGTON — President Trump told The Post in an interview this week that he doesn’t expect a surprise contender to shake up the 2028 Republican presidential primary — but that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is doing “a great job.”

Trump has spent the past year floating a choice between Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as his successor — seeming to enjoy fanning the guessing game.

Asked in the Oval Office Tuesday if he saw an unexpected contender emerging for the Republican nomination, Trump told The Post, “Probably not.”

“I mean, you have a certain group of people. I think it’s probably that’s the group. They’re very good. They call it a good bench,” he said.

But Trump then offered his praise for Hegseth when asked about the Pentagon chief being a candidate — a notion recently pushed forward by social influencers who have worked for his department, turning heads in DC.

“Well, I think he’s done a great job,” Trump replied. “I think he’s been treated very unfairly. Look, we had a war with Venezuela. It was over in one day. We lost nobody… We had Iran. We’re in month number eight, and we’ve lost 18 people.”

Trump brought both Vance and Rubio to the White House briefing room last Friday to bask in their praise of his trip to Asia for a historic trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The briefing, seen by some outlets as a tryout, concluded with Trump joking that Chief of Staff Stephen Miller outperformed both men and might himself be presidential material.

“I want to see how it all plays out. We have some very good people. We have some great people, really, but I just want to see how it plays out,” Trump told The Post. 

“It’s very early now, you know. It’s more than two years away. But it’s getting to be time where it’ll be all people are discussing. So I just want to see how it plays out.”

He didn’t float himself for a third term — an unconstitutional option that he’s used to troll Democrats.

The conventional wisdom in Washington for months has been that Vance is likely to run in 2028 and face an uphill battle against the Democratic nominee, with Rubio more likely to wait for the next presidential cycle should Vance lose.

But recent reporting has suggested Rubio, who ran as a traditional Republican against Trump’s populism in 2016 before becoming one of his closest advisers, is having second thoughts and might join the fray. 

Rubio’s stock has been rising since the midterms, with the RealClearPolitics average of polls now showing the Florida native surpassing Vance for the GOP 2028 presidential nomination after the VP had dominated the field all year.

A source close to the White House explained that Trump savors fomenting competition among his team and is likely to withhold his endorsement as long as possible — keeping himself in control of the party and postponing his own lame-duck status during the final two years of his term.

Trump declined to identify to The Post the Democrat he sees as toughest to beat in 2028 — but implied it wasn’t former Vice President Kamala Harris, whom he handily beat in 2024.

Polls suggest a hotly contested Democratic primary — with Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Harris in the upper tier.

“There are a couple of Democrats that I think would be tougher to beat than others,” Trump said — one day after he hosted a Justice Department event scorching Newsom for commuting the death sentences of serial killers.

“I don’t think I want to get into it, because if I do, I’m building them up. Well, maybe I can give you a false name, give you the opposite.”

Asked about Harris, the president smiled and added: “Kamala, Kamala. But she’s leading in the polls. Can you believe it?”
news.summary: Trump has spent the past year floating a choice between Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as his successor — seeming to enjoy fanning the guessing game.

news.title: Joe Biden's Memoir Is Full Of Easily Disproven Lies
news.text:
Authored by Matt Margolis via PJ Media,

Joe Biden has a long, well-documented record of fabricating and exaggerating his own biography, and he keeps repeating debunked stories as if saying them often enough could make them true.

For example, his son, Beau Biden, died of brain cancer at Walter Reed in 2015, yet Joe has repeatedly claimed that Beau "lost his life in Iraq."

And then there's another whopper he loves to tell about having an "epiphany" as a teenager that turned him into a champion of gay rights.

According to Biden, during his senior year of high school, his father dropped him off in Wilmington when they saw two men in suits kiss. "Joey, it's simple. They love each other," Biden claims his dad told him. He calls that moment the "epiphany" that shaped his views on same-sex marriage.

His actual record shows no such epiphany ever happened.

As a senator, Biden opposed letting gay people work in the federal government because he considered them a security risk. He backed "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" and voted for the Defense of Marriage Act, and even as vice president, he initially opposed civil unions for same-sex couples.

When a man spends decades lying about his past to build a political brand, it's inevitable that his presidential memoir will be full of whoppers too.

Sure enough, a Washington Free Beacon review by Jon Levine found that is loaded with factual errors and embellishments.

The biggest one involves Biden's first Senate run.

In the book, Biden wrote that he was "angered by a growing pattern of lies coming out of Washington" when he ran in 1972, and he named Richard Nixon's Watergate cover-up as one reason. The problem is the chronology doesn't support this fairy tale. The Watergate break-in happened on June 17, 1972, months after Biden had launched his Delaware Senate campaign.

Biden, then 29, formally declared his candidacy in January 1972, but he was already calling himself a "candidate" in 1971, and a November 1970 profile pegged him as a Democrat hopeful for the 1972 race. The scandal didn't unravel until the spring of 1973, and by then Biden had already won and taken the oath of office.

According to the Free Beacon, its line-by-line analysis turned up enough mistakes to suggest nobody ever fact-checked the book. And I'm sure that was intentional. A review in the U.K. Observer said the book is "rather obviously written by committee," produced by the same former West Wing operation that scripted Biden's presidency.

I don't think anyone actually believes Joe Biden wrote this book. I'm sure a bunch of people worked with him and his ghostwriter to bring it all together, but clearly, Biden's insistence on putting narratives before facts remains.

Take the American Rescue Plan Act. Biden wrote that the bill cleared the Senate on March 7 with Vice President Kamala Harris casting the tie-breaking vote, which he called "the first in a record number" of her tiebreakers.

However, the Senate actually passed it on March 6, 2021, by a 50-49 margin. So final passage did not need a tiebreaker. In fact, Kamala had already cast her first tie-breaking vote back in February 2021.

What a stupid thing to get wrong. And for what?

The border section is worse, since immigration is the issue that helped send Donald Trump back to the White House.

In the memoir, Biden called the February 2024 border deal "the toughest, most effective immigration and border bill ever put together," and he wrote that it would shut down the border if "more than four thousand people a week" tried to enter.

Not true. The actual bill would have triggered a shutdown at 5,000 crossings per day, or about 35,000 per week. Biden's version inflates the bill's toughness on an issue about which he faced bipartisan criticism for inaction.

The Free Beacon also found at least a dozen misstated dates and smaller errors. Biden placed his 2020 campaign kickoff rally in Philadelphia in April 2019, for example, even though it happened in May 2019, a date the book's own endnotes get right. Sloppy. Sloppy. Sloppy.

Telling lies about your story on the campaign trail or in an interview is bad enough. But people expect a stronger commitment to accuracy in a book. We're not talking about spinning a story in a positive way; we're talking about blatant factual errors and outright lies. That lack of interest in the truth in his presidential memoir, his final attempt to shape his presidential legacy, is a reflection of the dishonesty he's demonstrated throughout his career.

news.title: Guest columnist Gary Michael Tartakov: The kind of Democrat I voted for
news.text:
I was at an election night watch party, when one of our most articulate neighbors leaned over to another to worry about what he called the growing antisemitism in America, and the possible election of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. “I’m a Jew,” he said, “and I can tell you, Jews are not going to support a Democratic Party if it elects antisemitic candidates like El-Sayed.”

When someone chimed in about being critical of Israel not being antisemitic, my neighbor’s rejoinder was, “I’m critical of Israel, but El-Sayed has said things that are too insensitive and hostile to Jews.” (I will leave it to the reader to find quotes that actually fit those claims. I couldn’t.)

All the while I was trying to break in to point out that I was a Jew too, and that a significant part of the Jewish community rejected totally the idea that criticism of Israel was antisemitic. But my voice wasn’t getting any traction, so I’m burdening you with my typing skills here.

The actual situation in Michigan was reported on in the Times of Israel on Nov. 4, the day after the election. “DETROIT, Michigan — A small majority of Jews in Michigan backed the Democratic Party’s winning candidate, Abdul El-Sayed, over Republican Mike Rogers in Tuesday’s Senate race… Fifty-seven percent of Michigan Jews still backed him — though, tellingly, 78% of them supported the Democrats’ gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson, according to an exit poll of early voters.”

Exit polling good enough for an Israeli newspaper found that a majority of Michigan Jews voted for El-Sayed.

Think about Jewish Voice for Peace and others picketing at the Coolidge Bridge every Friday for the last three years. Or recognize that many if not most of the people in college and university encampments calling for a Palestinian state were Jews. 

It should now be clear to everyone that a large proportion of Jews do not accept the Zionist claim that people who criticize Israel are antisemites. Indeed, a large portion of the American criticism of Israel comes from Jews. Not the “self-hating Jews” that Zionists have invented, but Jews who have studied the history or just had the eyes to see the Israeli holocaust on Palestinians in Gaza for the atrocity that it continues to be.

The horrifying recent display of Israeli “settler” cruelty in the mainstream news is only a little more violent than that recorded in last year’s Oscar-winning documentary, and no different than documentation of settler violence driving Palestinians from their land that the left press has not ceased documenting since the 1940s.

Anyone who has read the history (or is willing to read the history) learns how Jewish criticism of Zionism for its intention to drive the people of Palestine from the land of their birth has existed as long as Zionism. The announced intention of Herzl’s Zionism was to carve out a Jewish state in Palestine by removing the people who lived there. The Jewish Labor Bund, founded the same year (1898), vociferously opposed the Zionist idea of displacing Palestinians in order to colonize Palestine.

The triumph of millions of dollars of ADL (Anti-Defamation League) and AIPAC (American Israel Political Action Committee) propaganda claiming to speak for all Jews has been to convince a great many that the way to be a friend to Jews was to support Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish-ruled state, where the 20% of the population that wasn’t Jewish had no say in the government, and all those captured in the Six Day War of 1967, had to give up their homes and fields to Israeli settlers.

The point I want to emphasize here is that despite the hundreds of millions of dollars spent by the ADL and AIPAC over the last three-quarters of a century to call criticism of Israel antisemitic, a large part of the Jewish community continues to be critical of Israel. And more importantly, they continue to be particularly critical of the United States subsidizing Israel’s terrorizing and murder of the Palestinians it has not been able to drive from Palestine, and Israel’s open war on the Palestinians that it has corralled into a barbed-wire-enclosed Gaza ghetto. 

Is there growing antisemitism in the Massachusetts or the United States? We cannot know, as the only statistics available are from the ADL, which counts criticism of Israel as antisemitic activity.

I’m not saying that the emotion-laden pleas of many people and politicians, such as Kamala Harris, that Israel has a right to defend itself, are not sincere. I’m saying that they were misled by the Zionist myth that the only way the Jewish people could be safe was to support Israel’s ethnic cleansing of Palestine.

Coming of age during the American war in Vietnam, I have spent my entire adult life fighting against our nation’s practice of bombing, or supporting allies in bombing non-white, non-Christian people, that our population is only painfully and slowly coming to recognize to be as entitled as we are to govern themselves, outside of our control. 

I don’t know how the Israelis and the Palestinians will eventually negotiate their shared occupation of the land of Palestine and Israel. I do know that they cannot develop that negotiation as long as the United States is providing Israel with unlimited arms, AI targeting intelligence, diplomatic immunity and financing that it has been.

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrats’ new senator from Michigan is someone I hope to hear a great deal more from, along with his predecessor on the current political scene, New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani: progressive Democrats who see a more working-class friendly world of Medicare for All, pre-K education, and a foreign policy that rejects U.S. funding of overseas wars attempting to maintain America’s economic superpower rule through allied business partners and the bombing of those that the U.S. public has not yet fully recognized as people, who deserve as much freedom of political choice, and justice as we do.

news.title: Trump Begs Reporters for Answers Following Midterm Losses as He Jokes 'Somebody Please Explain It to Me' During White House Speech
news.text:
President Donald Trump appeared perplexed by the results of the 2026 midterm elections, questioning how Republicans suffered significant losses after he won West Virginia by a wide margin in the 2024 presidential election, RadarOnline.com can report.

What is traditionally a lighthearted presidential holiday event also turned political as Trump touted his administration's accomplishments, discussed White House renovations, and expressed frustration over his party's losses.Turkey PardonsTrump pardoned two West Virginia-raised turkeys named Freedom and Feathers, raised by farmers Scott and Becky Reichel of Fort Seybert.

Only Freedom appeared at the ceremony; Feathers ran into the bushes beforehand, prompting Trump to acknowledge the bird’s disappearance.

After someone responded, "In the bushes," Trump decided both birds would receive a pardon. "But we'll give Feathers a pardon also, right? I think we better – we'll give them both," the president said.

He was joined by First Lady Melania Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson. Trump announced that both turkeys would receive a full pardon and travel to Texas A&M University’s Poultry Center.

He joked that the turkeys "will cheer on as the Aggies win games, game after game after game."

The 2026 ceremony marked the 79th presidential Thanksgiving turkey pardon; the annual tradition became established under President George H.W. Bush in 1989.Trump Begs for AnswersTrump shifted from the Thanksgiving celebration to politics, revisiting the Republican Party's performance in the November 3 midterm elections.

He brought up his 2024 victory in West Virginia, where he defeated Democrat Kamala Harris by approximately 45 percentage points.

"We won West Virginia by 45 points, at least I did when I was on the ballot. I don't know what happened. I won it by a lot,” Trump said.

He then asked for an explanation of what went wrong for Republicans.

"I don't know what the h-ll happened with this last election. Somebody please explain it to me," the 80-year-old asked. The remarks came after Democrats made significant gains and took control of both chambers of Congress.

Trump had spent much of his recent messaging promoting his administration’s economic record and urging support for Republican candidates.Administration Accomplishments and BallroomDuring the ceremony, Trump also praised his administration, claiming the country had experienced an exceptional period under his leadership.

He discussed the stock market, military investments, manufacturing, artificial intelligence, and data centers, while promoting the construction of the new White House ballroom.

He suggested next year's turkey-pardoning ceremony could take place inside the ballroom.Thanksgiving Is More Expensive Than Last YearThanksgiving dinner is more expensive in 2026 than it was last year, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's annual Thanksgiving dinner survey. 

The average cost of a traditional holiday meal for 10 people is estimated at $58.63, representing a 6 percent increase from 2025, or approximately $5.86 per person.

news.title: Why Republicans should worry about Gina Hinojosa in 2028
news.text:
RealClearPolitics’ latest polling average for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination has former Vice President Kamala Harris on top at 16.5%, followed by Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff at 15%, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 14% each, and California Gov. Gavin Newsom at 11.3%.

Years in Republican politics taught me never to say “never” about almost any candidate who jumps into the presidential ring. How many people truly saw Bill Clinton coming in 1992? Or Barack Obama in 2004? Or Donald Trump in 2014?

I’ve long urged the CEOs and politicians I’ve worked with to do something few are willing to do: Take off the partisan blinders and coldly, honestly assess not only their own weaknesses but also their rivals’ strengths.

Human nature makes that hard. None of us enjoys confronting our own flaws or crediting our adversaries. But in business and politics, brutally honest introspection – combined with an equally clear-eyed reading of the room – can give you a real advantage.

Practicing what I preach, I was most intrigued by a name missing from the RCP list: Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa.

A Texas earthquake Republicans didn’t see coming

Some on both sides of the aisle will say, “Give me a break. She’s a complete unknown next to the names on that list.” I’d bet the Democrats on that list are already taking her very seriously. And any potential Republican presidential candidate or operative who isn’t anticipating a populist groundswell behind Hinojosa is committing campaign malpractice.

Hinojosa is generating real buzz. Why?

To begin with, she crushed Republican Gov. Greg Abbott by more than 700,000 votes. In the U.S. Senate race, Democratic state legislator James Talarico held a narrow polling lead over the reputationally challenged Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton. But Abbott was expected to hang on – the final polling average had him up 3.5 percentage points. Hinojosa won by about 7.

Some chalk up that political spanking to the reviled Paxton dragging Abbott down with him. Others call it a win for voters fed up with President Trump, the Iran war and the cost of living. Did those factors play a role? Absolutely. But how about giving the winning candidate some credit, too?

Like him or not, Trump has long had that elusive “It Factor.” I and plenty of others have been saying so for a decade. You either have it or you don’t. It can’t be bought, taught or faked.

Because of it, Trump entered every presidential race with millions of votes already in his back pocket. Hinojosa is quickly developing that same quality.

The 2028 Electoral College math should scare the GOP

Then there’s the state she’ll start governing in January: Texas, with 40 electoral votes – second only to California’s 54.

Keep in mind that no Democratic presidential candidate has won Texas since Jimmy Carter in 1976. So the question going into 2028 is whether Democrats really turned Texas blue this year, or whether the wins by Hinojosa and Talarico were a one-off and the state will snap back to red. My bet is that if Hinojosa is on the ticket, it stays blue.

Should that come to pass, the math gets ugly for Republicans fast. Add Texas to the states Harris carried in 2024, and Democrats are at 266 electoral votes. Flip Michigan back, and they’re at 281.

Last time I checked, it takes 270 to win. Tell me again why so many Democrats want to scrap the Electoral College?

Next, the Hispanic vote. The nation’s Hispanic population hit 70.1 million last year, and it is growing and spreading across the country. As the first Latina governor of Texas, Hinojosa has made many in that community proud.

As for the knock that Hinojosa lacks experience, remember Obama. He went from community organizer to the Illinois Senate to the U.S. Senate in 2005, and he won the presidency less than four years later. Hinojosa is a former Austin school board president who was elected to the Texas House in 2016. In January, she’ll take over as governor of the nation’s second-largest state.

She also learned much of her politics at the feet of her father, Gilberto Hinojosa, a seasoned operative and former Cameron County judge who chaired the Texas Democratic Party from 2012 until 2025.

Finally, Hinojosa is already coming across as the adult in the room, someone willing to work across the aisle.

In a Fox News interview on Nov. 19, she said, “There is no question that it is because of President Trump that crossings have plummeted,” and that under former President Joe Biden, “there was chaos.” She also made clear that she thinks Immigration and Customs Enforcement has gone “too far.” Days earlier, she had called Trump to talk about border security.

I’ve long believed Americans are more than willing to elect a woman president. Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris didn’t lose because they were women. They lost because they were bad candidates.

Hinojosa has already made history in Texas. If I were Republican leadership, I’d be increasingly worried she could make more in November 2028. Be honest with yourselves, and read the room.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official and the author of “The 56: Liberty Lessons From Those Who Risked All to Sign the Declaration of Independence.”

news.title: New Data Suggests Majority Of Trump’s 2024 Base Abandoned GOP Over Party’s Support For Israel
news.text:
A majority of President Donald Trump’s 2024 supporters who abandoned him in the midterms believe he is too supportive of Israel, a new poll from Wednesday found. 

Fifty-six percent of 2024 Trump voters support blocking the transfer of bombs to Israel and 59% support reducing or ending all military aid to Israel, according to a survey by the Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) Policy Project. Voters largely disapproved of the Iran war heading into the midterm elections, which contributed to Democrats’ victories. 

Forty-two percent of voters who abandoned Trump said he is too supportive of Israel, while another 46% said he had the right level of support, according to the survey. 

The poll surveyed 636 Trump 2024 voters who either did not vote in the midterms or voted for a non-Republican candidate from Nov. 4 to Nov. 18 with a 4.3% margin of error. (RELATED: How The Generation Raised On Schindler’s List And Anne Frank Rethought Israel)

NEW POLL: A majority of Trump 2024 voters who abandoned Republicans in this year’s midterms support blocking bombs to Israel and stripping over $3 billion in annual taxpayer-funded weapons to Israel. These voters overwhelmingly believe the Iran war and US-Israel relationship benefits Israel more than the US. Read more from our poll conducted by YouGov below.— IMEU Policy Project (@imeupolicy) November 25, 2026

Young men and Latinos largely supported Democrats in 2026 after Trump made significant inroads with both groups in 2024. Fifty-eight percent of men ages 18 to 29 voted for Democrats, while 38% voted for Republicans, according to CIRCLE, a Tufts University survey. A Harvard Youth Poll found that young voters expected to be worse off financially than their parents for the first time in the poll’s history.

Generation Z showed the lowest levels of support for the Iran war among all generations surveyed by Navigator Research. Only 30% of Gen Z supported the war, while 44% of Baby Boomers and 55% of the Silent Generation supported Trump’s military actions.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other Israeli leaders urged Trump to enter the war during a meeting in the Situation Room in February. They laid out a plan to kill the ayatollah, destroy the Iranian military and institute regime change in Iran. 

Vice President J.D. Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA Director John Ratcliffe voiced skepticism of Israel’s plan for an attack and regime change. Trump remained set on the plan and believed the war would be short-lived. 

Fifty-eight percent of Latino men voted for Democrats, while 39% voted for Republicans, according to an NBC News exit poll. Latinos who voted for Democrats were primarily motivated by economic concerns. 

Sixty-one percent of voters identifying immigration as the top issue voted Republican, while 63% who prioritized the economy voted for Democrats, according to NBC News exit polling. 

Trump won the Latino male vote during the 2024 election, with 54% of Latinos voting for him over former Vice President Kamala Harris, a record for any Republican presidential candidate.

Hispanics shifted toward Democrats by 28 points since 2024, according to The New York Times. White voters shifted toward Democrats by 13 points, while young men ages 18 to 29 shifted toward Democrats by 41 points after they largely backed Trump in the last presidential election.

news.title: From Hollywood mogul to Biden-Harris insiders, Democrats turn to familiar faces to shape their next chapter
news.text: On the heels of the blue wave in the 2026 U.S. midterms, incoming Democratic leaders are tapping an eclectic mix of political veterans, business executives and entertainment figures to help shape their transitions into power. From a Hollywood mogul and former Biden administration officials to figures with ties to Republican leaders, the appointments offer an early glimpse into the people Democrats are turning to as they prepare to govern — and the experience and connections they hope to bring into their new administrations. Several incoming Democrats are turning to familiar faces from the Biden administration. In New Mexico, Gov.-elect Deb Haaland tapped former Biden presidential speechwriter Felicia Salazar and former Interior Department official Joan Mooney for her transition team, while California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra selected Arsenio Mataka, who previously served as his senior counselor at the Department of Health and Human Services under Biden, to direct policy for his transition team. In Ohio, Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton tapped Elisabeth Hire, a former aide to then-Vice President Biden, as a transition co-chair. Haaland's campaign and Becerra's campaign each did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The transition teams will help incoming leaders prepare to take office, including identifying potential administration officials, shaping policy priorities and laying the groundwork for their first days in power. The selections also offer a window into the experience, relationships and perspectives newly elected Democrats are turning to as they prepare to govern. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., tapped Egyptian-American lawyer Brenda Abdelall as the director of his transition team, Politico Playbook first reported in early November. Abdelall previously claimed that Zionists were "controlling" much of U.S. politics, The Washington Free Beacon reported Nov. 6, though Harris' 2024 presidential campaign said at the time that the remarks did not reflect Abdelall's current views. "The Zionists have a strong voice in American politics," Abdelall told the New York Sun during a conference for the American Muslim Council in 2002, the Free Beacon reported. "I would say they're controlling a lot of it." Abdelall previously served as the assistant secretary of partnership and engagement at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. She also directed the Kamala Harris 2024 presidential campaign's outreach to Arab American voters, Reuters reported. JEWISH LEADERS IN MICHIGAN PREPARE TO WORK WITH ABDUL EL-SAYED DESPITE LINGERING CONCERNS El-Sayed campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner told Fox News Digital on Nov. 9 that Abdelall "comes to the role of transition director with decades of experience leading teams at the highest levels of politics, including the Biden-Harris administration." "While at the Department of Homeland Security, Brenda worked to implement the nation’s first National Strategy to Counter Antisemitism and frequently spearheaded efforts to counter the rise of hate crimes and violence across the country," Richner added. "The transition team is committed to building a team that reflects the great diversity of Michigan and ensuring that the El-Sayed office serves all communities across the state." El-Sayed is set to assume office on Jan. 3, 2027. Perry has long been known for his philanthropic efforts, including supporting underserved communities and charitable causes across Georgia. Bottoms lauded Perry as "an entertainment mogul who is also a huge philanthropic part of our Georgia community and owns Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta," WDSU reported. EX-BIDEN OFFICIAL WINS GEORGIA DEM PRIMARY FOR GOVERNOR IN BID TO END PARTY'S LOSING STREAK The news that Perry will serve on Bottoms’ Georgia transition team has sparked some criticism due to the entertainment mogul facing two active lawsuits accusing him of sexual assault and misconduct, allegations his attorneys have denied, Variety reported Nov. 6. Greg Abbott, and Thaddeus Cleveland, a Republican sheriff from Terrell County, as part of his transition team, according to the Chronicle.
