news.title: How the Gaza Encampments Unleashed the Blue Tsunami and Helped Spark a Worldwide Movement
news.text:
The Hidden Backstory of the Blue Wave

Students at Columbia University set up tents on the lawn at the center of campus in April 2024 and said they would stay until the university divested from Israel’s war on Gaza. Within weeks, encampments had spread to campuses across the country, and soon around the world.

I was a law student at Columbia that spring and spent much of it in the encampment. I remember the cold nights and the teach-ins on the grass, the food that kept arriving from strangers, a Passover seder held on the lawn, and students praying in rows beside the tents. 

Those who watched from a distance may remember a different set of images: riot police dragging students across their own campuses, an Emory economics professor thrown to the ground by officers, and a spring in which more than 2,000 people were arrested at protests nationwide. By the summer, the tents were gone. The bombing of Gaza continued.

In the 2024 presidential race, these same young people who had spent the spring organizing were asked to support a ticket that would not break with the policy they had protested. They were told that their objection was a luxury the country could not afford. Months before the encampments, more than 100,000 Michigan Democrats had voted “uncommitted” to warn the party about Israel’s onslaught, but the warning went largely unheeded. Many of us voted that November with dread, and some could not bring themselves to vote at all.

Donald Trump won the presidency, and within only a few months, federal immigration agents had detained Mahmoud Khalil (who had negotiated on the encampment’s behalf), and Columbia had agreed to pay more than $200 million to the administration that was punishing its students. By then, much of the commentary class had decided the protests had alienated voters and might even have helped elect Trump.

The midterm election results told a very different story. Darializa Avila Chevalier, who was arrested alongside students at Columbia’s encampment in 2024, won the congressional seat that includes the university, after unseating a five-term incumbent in June’s primary. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, who ran openly against his own party’s position on Gaza, won a seat in the Senate. Democrats took back both the House and the Senate, and they did it by winning in places the party had stopped imagining it could compete: Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, to name a few, while also flipping Senate seats in Ohio and Maine. When Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor of New York City a year ago, plenty of commentators treated it as a local story, one that could only happen there; the midterm results show they were wrong.

This election was enormous, and the encampments belong at the center of the story of how it happened. Gaza was the source of the anger: For two years, a generation watched the genocide on their phones in real time, while the people they had been raised to trust explained why nothing could be done. The encampments and the wider student movement gave that anger somewhere to go, taught people how to organize, and even more importantly, showed them the institutions meant to protect them simply would not. If young people wanted to be represented, we realized we would have to build that representation ourselves.

Learning From the Encampments

Many of the students who joined the encampments had never organized anything before. Within days — especially after the original organizers were arrested — they were running a small town: rotating security shifts, feeding hundreds of people, coordinating legal observers and jail support, holding meetings late into the night to decide by consensus what to do next, and negotiating with administrators who had far more power than they did.

Students learned how to bring a demand to an institution, how to build a coalition across groups that did not always agree, and how to keep people together after arrests and suspensions. Jewish, Muslim, Arab, Black, and Latino students, graduate workers, faculty, and neighbors from Harlem and Morningside Heights in New York City learned to work beside one another. Political campaigns run on those same skills, and plenty of people who staffed jail-support lines in 2024 were staffing phone banks two years later.

Socialist organizers were part of that education from the start. Members of the Young Democratic Socialists of America helped set up encampments from the University of California, Berkeley to New York City’s Hunter College, and the culture there — with mass meetings, shared labor, and decisions made together — already resembled the organizing that the Democratic Socialists of America had been practicing in tenant unions and on picket lines for years.

The students also learned what their universities would do when tested. Columbia presented itself as a place for open debate and then called the police on its own students, suspended and expelled them, and later settled with the federal government to restore its funding while one of the encampment’s negotiators sat in immigration detention. Students who had been taught that their schools existed to protect free inquiry watched those schools choose their endowments and their relationships with power instead. Many of them had already watched law firms withdraw job offers from students who had signed statements about Gaza in the fall of 2023. The lesson was harsh and clarifying: No institution was coming to save them.

The Democratic Party gave them no reason to think otherwise. Even after Biden withdrew and Kamala Harris became the nominee, the policy stayed where it was, and at the party’s convention that August, organizers rejected the Uncommitted delegates’ request to have a Palestinian American speak on the main stage.

For a generation already disillusioned with their universities, this confirmed that if Gen Z wanted their voices heard in the halls of power, they would need to knock on the doors, recruit the candidates, raise the money through small donations, and build the organizations themselves.

From the Lawn to the Ballot

Mamdani’s mayoral campaign was the first clear sign that they had started that work. He grew out of that energy, and his campaign gave it a direction. His primary victory in June 2025 rested on years of organizing by tenants, socialists, workers, and Palestine solidarity groups, and much of it ran through New York City DSA, whose electoral organizers described the coalition behind him as young New Yorkers becoming politically active, tenants, and voters drawn to both his affordability agenda and his support for Palestinian rights.

Sociologist Heba Gowayed traced the protest movement’s contribution to his win within days of the result. More than 50,000 people signed up to volunteer during that primary. Many of them were young people who had never knocked on a door for a candidate before, and they learned to canvass the way they had learned to run an encampment: quickly, from one another, and because no one else was going to do it for them. A campaign that talked about both affordability and Palestinian rights gave them a reason to give up their evenings and weekends. When he won the general election, more than 2 million New Yorkers had voted, the most in a mayoral race since 1969.

Mamdani’s victory changed what seemed possible for everyone watching. Candidates who had been warned that criticizing Israel would end their careers could now point to New York. Reps. Rashida Tlaib and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, currently the only members of DSA in Congress, will be joined by a record number of DSA-endorsed candidates, at least six. Claire Valdez, a state assembly member who had joined protests calling for an arms embargo on Israel, won the open seat in New York’s 7th Congressional District. In Colorado, Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old lawyer who lost her job after refusing to take down a social media post criticizing law firms over their positions on Israel and Palestine, unseated Rep. Diana DeGette, who had held the seat for three decades.

Avila Chevalier remains the clearest line from the lawn to the Capitol. She is a Columbia alumna who stood with students through arrests and threats of expulsion, and who had spent years in immigrant rights and community organizing before that spring. She ran with the backing of the same democratic socialists who had helped elect Mamdani. After her primary, Maryam Alwan, who protested at Columbia in 2024 (and with whom I am proud to have studied at Sciences Po Menton in France), told Al Jazeera what it meant to see “Darializa, a former leader and organiser of the encampment, represent the school that arrested her.” Gowayed, the sociologist, put the connection more bluntly: “This does not happen if those students don’t encamp; it just doesn’t happen.”

In Michigan, the state where the uncommitted vote first registered the party’s Gaza problem, Seed the Vote organized Jewish, Muslim, and Arab volunteers to knock doors for El-Sayed together, alongside IfNotNow and Bend the Arc. El-Sayed spoke directly to voters’ anger over the party’s position on Gaza and asked them to elect someone who shared it. 

For anyone who had been in the encampments, those canvasses would have looked familiar. Khalil, who was released from detention in June 2025 and is still facing deportation, pointed to El-Sayed and Mamdani a week before the election as evidence that politics was shifting. “The American public is finally changing, is finally looking at the Palestinian as an equal human,” he said.

Anger at Trump, the cost of living, and organizations with decades of history all helped produce the blue tsunami, and no election return can isolate the share owed to the encampments. For people who had already concluded that their leaders were willing to fund devastation in Gaza while claiming there was no money for housing or healthcare at home, the war with Iran confirmed the judgment. 

By October, polls compiled by Responsible Statecraft found voters were more worried about the war than about immigration or crime, and 6 in 10 opposed U.S. military action against Iran. The candidates who won on Election Day week treated rent, healthcare, and war as one argument about whose lives the government is willing to sacrifice, and young voters answered them.

Lessons for Serbia and India

Americans were not the only ones to see a student movement reach the ballot this fall. In November 2024, the canopy of the Novi Sad railway station collapsed and killed 16 people, and Serbian students, blaming the corruption they believed had made the disaster possible, blockaded their faculties and demanded accountability. Inside the blockades, they ran themselves through plenums and open assemblies with no leaders; every decision went to a vote. In March 2025, they invited the rest of the country to do the same, and within 10 days, citizens had formed their own assemblies, called zborovi, in neighborhoods and towns from Niš to Novi Sad. That same month, roughly 300,000 people filled Belgrade for the largest protest in Serbia’s history, but a moment of silence for the victims ended in panic when the crowd scattered from what protesters and analysts said was a sonic weapon; the government denied using one.

In May 2025, the students began calling for snap parliamentary elections. Serbian opposition politics had long concentrated on the cities and left smaller towns and villages to the ruling party, so the students went there, knocking on doors in places where the state media had branded them terrorists. On October 25, almost two years after the collapse, the Students’ List group won 140 of Parliament’s 250 seats and ended Aleksandar Vučić’s party’s hold on government. The plenums had taught them how to make decisions together, keep thousands of people moving in the same direction, and earn trust one conversation at a time — skills they carried over into election campaigning. Few people would have predicted that outcome during the first winter of the blockades, when the students were being dismissed as naïve.

In India, young people organized under the banner of the Cockroach Janta Party have been in the streets since September, together with student groups and opposition parties, protesting a revision of the voter rolls that has removed more than 130 million names. Police have detained thousands of them, and it would be easy to judge that movement by what it wins this month. Two years from now, we may have a better sense of what it set in motion.

What Comes Next

Nothing that happened on Election Day can repair what was done to Gaza, and the encampments’ original demands remain unmet. The students were protesting the killing of Palestinians and their own institutions’ complicity in it, and electing a former organizer to Congress will not change American policy toward Israel on its own. The organizations that carried these candidates into office will need to stay independent enough to press them once they arrive, and the voters who returned to the Democratic Party this year came back on conditions. Officials who forget this should expect the same organizers to come for their seats.

For those of us who felt crushed in 2024, though, the midterm victories deserve to be fully absorbed and celebrated. We were told that the protests had failed, that we had cost the party an election, that our anger was a liability. The people who had every reason to give up kept meeting instead. They recruited friends, built campaigns, found candidates they could believe in, and spent two years knocking on doors in neighborhoods where no one expected them. 

While the news cycle may measure movements in weeks, it wrote this one off before most of its participants had graduated. The verdict came on Election Day, two years late, and it was written by the same people who had been dismissed. We did it, or at least we started to. The work ahead is harder, and it will take longer than anyone would like, but it starts now, with the wind at our backs.

news.title: Americans Didn't Vote for Socialism in the Midterms. They Voted Against Republicans.
news.text:
As America approached the midterms, my wish was simple: An election result so resounding that no one could doubt its meaning. Trump 2.0 has been a disaster for those of us who value free trade, democratic norms, limited government, and freedom across the globe. If voters didn't rebuke the president and instead gave some murky verdict by, say, handing Democrats a few modest wins, then nothing would change.

The results seem hard to miss, even if a few MAGA types have tried to spin them as a normal midterm rejection of the governing party. Democrats flipped nine U.S. Senate seats for a 56-44 majority. They gained around 45 U.S. House seats and will have an 83-plus seat majority. Democrats won six governorships and flipped hundreds of state legislative seats. Democrats' victories in Texas would be the equivalent of Republicans running the table in California. It was a bloodbath.

Yet political takes vary widely. Republicans are doubling down, with Donald Trump elevating Stephen Miller—the Nosferatu-like architect of the administration's aggressive ICE policies—to White House chief of staff. The Never Trump movement is squabbling between its conservative and Democratic-aligned factions. And Democrats are warring between liberals and democratic socialists. So much for getting back to that center-left/center-right pre-Trump consensus.

The dumbest Democratic take comes from those aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). "From coast to coast, American voters have emphatically endorsed socialism to oppose the corruption and barbarism of Donald Trump and the Republicans," the group wrote in a statement. Certainly, Americans widely rejected the president's corruption and abuses, but that's the equivalent of saying American voters emphatically endorsed cannibalism in doing so.

DSA is basically the Left's version of MAGA—an economically ignorant group, filled with grievances and out of touch with most Americans. I was reading X after Mississippi voters decided to pick another senator, and one leftist warned his fellow travelers that Democratic senator-elect Scott Colom is—shocking!—a pro-gun moderate and former prosecutor. Well, yes, that's why he won in one of the most conservative states in the nation. All these fringe movements value in-group purity over victory.

Even some conservative pundits have jumped on the "socialists have taken over" bandwagon, but that's probably easily explained by the doom and gloom people often feel after defeat. (It's a particularly funny take given that they're making it as the president they support is gushing over China's communist leader Xi Jinping and former KGB-chief-turned-dictator Vladimir Putin.)

Everyone needs to calm down and take a close look at the post-election numbers. CNN ran them and found Democratic candidates from the party's moderate wing vastly outperformed DSAers, many of whom dragged down the party: "(I)n key races, the four candidates most aligned with the party's left flank—and endorsed by influential democratic socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont—accounted for the four worst performances, compared to 2024."

The far-left's most prominent candidates barely outperformed Kamala Harris' 2024 numbers, whereas, "The average Democratic Senate candidate in key races ran 16 points better than Harris did in 2024." Certainly, the network noted, DSA candidates can win in the most progressive districts, but they fare poorly outside of these ideological hothouses.

For example, Democrats are routinely frustrated by Florida, where each election they believe they have a shot at making inroads. Florida is a conservative state, yet a key reason for the Democratic Senate loss this election is that the party ran state Rep. Angie Nixon, a member of the DSA and the far-left Working Families Party. Her underwhelming opponent, Ashley Moody, won by 3 percentage points—so it was one of Democrats' squandered opportunities.

DSA is an anchor around the Democratic Party, not its savior. Do you wonder why? I went to the DSA website and followed a link to the Socialist Forum, which yammered about its efforts "confronting the tensions and contradictions of advancing socialism within an imperialist capitalist society from within the halls of capitalist governance itself."

Yikes. Normal Americans don't think or talk that way. Normal Americans are most likely to embody what author Ronald Wright quipped (paraphrasing John Steinbeck): "Socialism never took root in America because the poor see themselves not as an exploited proletariat but as temporarily embarrassed millionaires." It's not going to take root now.

That said, some DSA-aligned politicians, such as New York City's Mayor Mamdani, have mostly governed as ordinary big-city liberals. Los Angeles' incoming Mayor Nithya Raman won against an incumbent whose post-wildfire incompetence roiled local politics. But Raman distanced herself from DSA and campaigned as a government reformer. I'm not thrilled about the emergence of any DSA officials, but reality will moderate those with ambition.

The post-mortems are not that hard. The Trump administration vastly overreached. So voters picked the only alternative by handing Democrats big victories. If Democrats ever believe that Americans want socialism, they better get used to losing again.

This column was first published in The Orange County Register.
news.summary: Democrats won the midterms despite the DSA, not because of it.
news.author: Steven Greenhut

news.title: AOC’s 2028 Chances Against Jon Ossoff As She Surges With DSA Members
news.text: U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York is leading a push among Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members to secure the organization's endorsement for a 2028 presidential run, with 671 sign-ons to a petition. Meanwhile, U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia holds a narrow advantage in national polling and prediction markets. Neither politician has declared a presidential campaign. Ocasio-Cortez, 37, has left the possibility open, while Ossoff has explicitly said he will not run. “My focus is on doing what’s best for people,” the New York congresswoman said when asked about 2028. “I’m less about the horse race. You know, these elections just happened. Let’s get some results for people first, and then we can talk about elections later.” And during an October debate in Georgia, Ossoff pledged to serve a full six-year term if reelected. “I have zero interest in running for president,” the 39-year-old senator said. “I’m not running for president.” Newsweek emailed both Ocasio-Cortez and Ossoff’s offices for further comment on Friday morning. Why It Matters The contrast captures a choice Democrats could eventually face between Ocasio-Cortez’s strength among organized progressives and Ossoff’s potential appeal across a broader electorate. Key Points Sponsored by Kalshi Ocasio-Cortez Clears the DSA Threshold The DSA began its search for a potential 2028 candidate after making gains in the midterm elections. Its National Political Committee (NPC) explained the endorsement process during a November 18 mass call event. Ocasio-Cortez’s total makes her the only person in the reported field to have crossed the qualifying mark. According to Democratic Left, a publication affiliated with the organization, prospective nominees must collect signatures through the DSA Endorsement Hub before a Presidential Exploratory Committee decides whether to approve them. Ocasio-Cortez had received more than five times Tlaib’s total and over nine times Fain’s as of November 22, the publication reported. The count is not a DSA endorsement, a representative membership poll or evidence of support across the Democratic electorate. It shows that Ocasio-Cortez has enough backing among participating members to clear the first procedural hurdle. Ossoff Holds a Narrow Polling Edge Emerson College’s latest national survey offers a broader, though still extremely early, view of Democratic preferences. When respondents were shown a list of possible candidates, Ossoff received 17 percent, followed by former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris at 16 percent, Ocasio-Cortez at 15 percent and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 14 percent. Outgoing California Governor Gavin Newsom took 11 percent, Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear 7 percent, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly 4 percent, with Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker each at 3 percent. The gaps separating the leading four contenders fall within the survey’s uncertainty range, meaning the results identify a competitive top tier rather than a clear front-runner. In the open-ended version, which asked voters to volunteer a name without seeing options, Ossoff remained on 17 percent while Ocasio-Cortez fell to 12 percent. That difference suggests the Georgia senator may currently have greater spontaneous salience, while a prompted list benefits several better-known alternatives. Emerson surveyed 1,000 U.S. voters from November 14 to 16. The poll, published November 19, carried a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A separate Reuters/Ipsos study measured perceived candidate quality rather than primary voting intention. Ossoff and Buttigieg were each rated an “excellent” potential nominee by 29 percent of Democrats, illustrating that favorable impressions do not necessarily translate into a settled choice. That survey questioned 1,705 U.S. adults, including roughly 500 registered voters from each party, from November 6 to 9. Results among Democratic and Republican voters had margins of error of plus or minus 5 percentage points. Traders Prefer Ossoff Prediction markets pointed in the same general direction as of 6 a.m. ET on Friday, November 27. Kalshi contracts priced Ossoff’s chance of winning the 2028 presidential election at 17 percent, compared with 12 percent for Ocasio-Cortez and 11 percent for Vice President JD Vance. More than $115 million had been traded in the market. Polymarket placed the Georgia senator at 18 percent, ahead of Vance on 12 percent, Ocasio-Cortez on 11 percent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on 9 percent. Unlike surveys, those figures reflect prices set by people buying and selling contracts. They can incorporate expectations about whether someone will run, survive the primaries and win the Electoral College, but thin liquidity or sudden news can distort individual outcomes. What Happens Next Approved DSA nominees are due to appear at a presidential town hall between February 15 and 28, 2027. “Nominees will be invited to a town hall discussion for DSA leaders and members to ask questions about how their campaign, and perhaps even their administration, will shape the course of American history,” NPC member Sidney Carlson White said. The NPC is expected to make the final recommendation between March and May, although the timetable could change depending on candidate announcements. NPC member and union organizer Sarah Milner said any presidential bid would be intended to strengthen a wider working-class movement, with chapters preparing candidates throughout the 2028 ballot rather than concentrating their resources on a single race. “With millions of people looking for someone to lead, it is up to DSA to answer the call,” Milner said. “Prepare your chapter, not just to elect one candidate, but to build a movement that can overturn this whole corrupt system.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Sam Stevenson and Cristina Diciu.
news.summary: Neither has entered the race, but socialist enthusiasm for AOC contrasts with Jon Ossoff’s early advantage in polls and markets.

news.title: Where 2026’s ‘blue tsunami’ voters came from — and where they could be in 2028
news.text:
Two years after President Donald Trump won the popular vote by 1.5 percentage points, Democrats won the national popular vote for the House by about 14. That’s a swing of more than 15 points, the second-largest for any party out of power since World War II.

How did the Democrats pull this off? In election analytics, I often break down changes in elections due to two forces: vote-switching and turnout. Every vote a former Republican voter casts for a Democrat counts as a switch, whereas Republicans sitting out — or Democrats voting at higher-than-normal rates — count as a turnout edge.

In 2026, Democrats’ voters turned out at far higher rates than Republicans’, and some of Trump’s voters switched sides. The analysis in this article suggests about 40% of the overall 15.5-point swing to Democrats between 2024 and 2026 was due to vote-switching, and about half was due to changes in turnout among people who voted in 2024. The last 10% came from new voters, which can be seen as both a turnout effect and a vote-switching, or persuasion, effect.

If you’re wondering what 2026 means for 2028, I’m using data to show how reasonable assumptions about the persistence of 2024-2026 vote-switching and the Democratic turnout could forecast 2028 — which could likely wind up anywhere from a close race to a Democratic blowout.

Inevitably, a reader will wonder what this all means for 2028. There is no firm answer, but I can speculate about certain outcomes that would happen if you make certain assumptions about how persistent the vote-switching and turnout patterns are over the next two years.

About one-third of Trump’s 2024 supporters stayed home

To separate turnout from switching, I used the MS NOW Voter Poll, which interviewed voters before and during Election Day and is adjusted to be representative of the outcome of the election. Its national House results tables show how each group of 2024 voters voted this year. Among Kamala Harris’ voters, for example, 97% of those who turned out again backed a Democrat, and 2% picked a Republican. Among Trump’s, 7% backed a Democrat and 91% a Republican. People who didn’t vote in 2024 went Democratic, 71% to 25%.

I estimated the percentage of the swing in the election that is due to vote-switching in two steps.

First, I reweighed the results of the Voter Poll to be representative of the 2024 election by recalled vote, in effect imagining what would have happened if everyone who voted in 2024 voted again. In this hypothetical, 2024 Trump voters still outnumbered Harris voters by 1.5 points, but each group voted the way it did this year. In this hypothetical, Democrats won the 2026 House vote by about 4.6 points. That made for a 6-point swing (4.6 points plus 1.5 points) that I could attribute to vote-switching alone. About 5 points of this came from 2024 Trump voters-switching to Democrats, and about 1 point from 2024 third-party voters switching to Democrats.

Then, I subtracted that statistic (six-point swing) from the total swing in the 2026 election. But Democrats won by 14 — a total 15.5-point swing from the 2024 election. If the six-point swing was due to vote-switching, the other 9.5 points must come from the mix of voters who actually showed up. I estimated that about eight points came from 2024 Harris voters returning at higher rates than Trump’s, and 1.5 points from new voters who were extremely likely to vote for Democrats (according to the MS NOW Voter Poll, 2024 nonvoters chose Democrats by 46 points). That’s about 40% of the swing from switching, about half from turnout among 2024 voters and about 10% from new voters.

I can also do this math in raw votes instead of percentages. Of the roughly 68 million votes for Democratic House candidates, about 59 million came from Harris voters, 3.7 million from Trump voters who switched, 3.5 million from new voters and the rest from people who voted third-party in 2024. So about 61 million of Harris’ 75 million voters came back to the polls (59 million voting for Democrats), or 81%, and nearly all of them voted Democratic. Only 52 million of Trump’s 77 million did, or 68%.

Sixty-eight percent is actually a remarkable turnout level for a midterm. In the 2022 midterms, by the same math, about 65% of each side’s 2020 voters participated again. So Trump’s voters didn’t really skip this election any more than usual, Harris’ just massively outperformed.

Vote-switching was higher for more moderate candidates

I repeated the exercise above, which used national Voter Poll numbers, at the state level for every Senate race to break down how each voter said they voted in 2024. As before, if the 2024 voters who showed up in 2026 were more Democratic than in 2024, that implies a turnout edge among Democrats in that state, with Republicans disproportionately staying home.

There were significant differences across states in the split between turnout and vote-switching. For example, Trump carried North Carolina by three points in 2024, but this year’s voters there recalled backing Harris by six. He carried Texas by 14, and this year’s Texas voters recalled backing him by just five.

In North Carolina’s Senate race, vote-switching alone turned Trump's three-point win into a nine-point Democratic lead. Turnout and new voters took it the rest of the way, to a 20-point tilt in Democrats’ favor.

But the vote-switching rate varied wildly across states, from 4% of Trump voters backing the Democratic candidate in Minnesota and Maine, and 6% in Michigan, to 13% in Georgia, 11% in Texas and 10% in North Carolina.

Why did some Democrats win three times as many Trump voters as others?

One plausible answer is that Trump voters were less willing to cross the aisle for nominees who were viewed as more extreme. The Voter Poll asked whether each Democrat's views were “too extreme,” and the answers at the state level correlate highly with the corresponding vote-switching rates.

For example, the three Senate Democrats least likely to be called too extreme were Jon Ossoff, Georgia’s incumbent senator (34%); Roy Cooper, North Carolina's former two-term governor (37%); and Chris Pappas, a four-term New Hampshire congressman (38%). They won 13%, 10% and 7% of Trump voters.

At the other end were Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota's lieutenant governor, who both ran with the backing of the party's progressive wing. Of the 11 Democratic Senate candidates the poll asked about, they were the only ones called too extreme by more voters than had backed Trump in their states. They won 6% and 4% of Trump voters.

But before making sweeping claims about how ideology interacts with vote-switching and turnout, note a prominent exception. Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas was viewed as too extreme by 46% of Texans (versus 47% who voted for Trump in 2024), and he still won 11% of Trump voters.

What 2026 implies for the 2028 presidential map

Inevitably, a reader will wonder what this all means for 2028. There is no firm answer, but I can speculate about certain outcomes that would happen if you made certain assumptions about how persistent the vote-switching and turnout patterns are over the next two years.

To turn these numbers into 2028 projections, I first made the assumption that vote-switching will be constant across years and held this year’s vote choices fixed within each group, so every Trump voter who crossed over stayed crossed over.

Then, I changed only who turned out — all 2024 Trump drop-off voters, only the new voters or some of both. I used the numbers from each state with a Senate race, plus the governor races in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Arizona and Nevada, which had no Senate contest but did elect a governor this year. For every other state, I applied the national switching rates to the state's 2024 electorate.

This produces four scenarios:

The 2024 electorate. Harris, Trump and third-party voters turn out in their 2024 proportions in each state, and this year’s new voters stay home. Democrats’ turnout edge disappears entirely. This is the switching-only step from above.

2024 plus new voters. The voters who skipped 2024 (about 4% of this year's electorate nationally, and Democratic by 46 points) come back, at half that margin.

Half the turnout edge survives. Same, but the turnout gap between Harris and Trump voters closes only halfway.

The 2024 electorate with only half of vote-switching. The bear case for Democrats. Same as the first scenario, but half of this year’s switchers go back to the party they backed in 2024.

Here’s what each scenario implies for the Democratic vote margin in each state that had a competitive statewide election this year:

Even with the turnout edge gone completely, Democrats lead the national House vote by about 5 points, larger than Joe Biden’s 2020 winning vote margin. In this scenario, Georgia, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Arizona go blue.

Counting any state within 3 points as a toss-up, Democrats win 296 electoral votes with no turnout edge at all, with another 86 in toss-ups, including Michigan and Texas. That’s more than the 270 they need before a single toss-up is counted. With new voters back, Michigan moves into their column, for 311. If half the turnout edge survives, Texas does too, for 353, and the toss-ups stretch to Kansas, South Carolina and Alaska.

The bear case is the only one that leaves the election in doubt. With the 2024 electorate and only half of this year’s switching, Democrats lead nationally by less than 2 points and win 261 electoral votes, nine short of a majority. The other 58 they would be fighting for are in Michigan, North Carolina, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada, all within 3 points.

I would consider this a sort of “bull case” for the Democrats, since it involves holding constant the vote-switching rates for Senate candidates who may fit their state much better than the national presidential candidate in 2028 will.

In a fourth scenario where Democrats keep only half of their Trump converts, they would win the national popular vote by 1.6 points and “just” 261 electoral votes, nine short of 270. States worth 58 electoral votes would be toss-ups: Michigan (+0.1), Arizona (−0.1), Wisconsin (+1.6), Nevada (−2.6) and North Carolina (+2.7).

But history points to the higher end of that range. In the nine midterms since WWII where the party out of power swung the House vote by 9 points or more, its House margin fell by about five points on average in the next presidential election. Knock five off this year's 14 and you get nine, almost exactly the half-turnout-edge scenario.

The 2028 Senate map looks surprisingly good for Democrats

Democrats will hold 56 Senate seats in January. In 2028, they will defend 16 and Republicans 18, counting the Ohio and Florida seats filled by special elections this year. Using each state’s 2026 numbers as a stand-in for 2028, I get the following simulated Senate results:

In the three scenarios that keep all of this year’s switching, Democrats flip North Carolina and Wisconsin, and the two seats they could lose, Ohio and Nevada, are toss-ups. So they end up with at least 56 seats, the number they hold now. With no turnout edge at all, Iowa is a toss-up, too, and they could reach 59. Keep half the edge, and Kansas, South Carolina and Alaska join the toss-ups, for as many as 62.

The bear case is rougher. With only half the switching, Democrats lose Ohio, and North Carolina, Wisconsin, Arizona and Nevada are all toss-ups. That leaves them with 53 to 57 seats — still a comfortable majority.

This exercise gave us a sense of what a 2028 election could look like if Democrats repeat their success with vote-switchers who powered the “blue tsunami” this year. Even with every bit of Democrats’ turnout edge erased, they would still be favored to win nationally and above an expected 270 electoral votes.

If half of this year’s converts drift back, too, they would be nine electoral votes short, with the election riding on five toss-up states. And in the Senate, they could expand their already impressive majority.

But handicapping an election two years out comes with a large margin of error. These scenarios hold this year’s vote choices fixed, and converts can drift back. Two years ago, nobody thought Democrats could win 56 Senate seats, and in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Mississippi and South Carolina, of all places. A lot can change in two years, but this gives us a good idea of where the electoral environment starts.

news.title: Biden celebrates Memoir’s No. 1 Bestseller triumph
news.text:
WASHINGTON-(MaraviPost)-Former United States President Joe Biden is celebrating a major literary milestone after his presidential memoir, Promise Me, America, secured the number-one position on The New York Times bestseller list, giving the former Democratic leader a fresh opportunity to reconnect with readers and reflect on his four years in the White House.

According to a statement shared by Biden on his official social media account, he expressed gratitude to readers for supporting the book, describing its commercial success as a reflection of their willingness to engage with his account of America’s political, economic and international journey under his administration.

The achievement comes barely days after the memoir’s release on November 17, 2026, and represents a significant commercial breakthrough for Biden, whose latest publication revisits his presidency from January 2021 to January 2025.

In his message, Biden wrote: “I am humbled and honored that PROMISE ME, AMERICA is #1 on the New York Times bestseller list, and that’s because of you.” He thanked readers for embracing the publication and helping it reach the top of one of America’s most influential literary rankings.

The former president explained that his central motivation for writing the memoir was to document what he considers the collective achievements of his administration, particularly its efforts to improve economic opportunities for ordinary Americans and strengthen the country’s international standing.

He specifically highlighted his administration’s commitment to giving working families a fair opportunity to improve their economic circumstances, presenting the book as an account of policies and decisions intended to expand prosperity and restore confidence in American leadership.

Published by Little, Brown and Company, Promise Me, America examines Biden’s four years in office, including his domestic policy priorities, economic interventions, international relations, diplomatic challenges and the political decisions that shaped his presidency.

The publisher announced that the 480-page memoir would provide Biden’s personal account of the defining events of his administration, including the challenges surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic, economic recovery, infrastructure investment, the war in Ukraine and America’s response to international conflicts.

However, the memoir also revisits one of the most controversial chapters of Biden’s political career: his decision to seek re-election in 2024 before eventually withdrawing from the presidential race following mounting pressure over his age and performance during a televised debate against Donald Trump.

His decision to step aside cleared the way for then-Vice President Kamala Harris to become the Democratic presidential candidate, although she subsequently lost the election to Trump.

In its assessment of the memoir, Britain’s The Guardian observed that Biden offers substantial accounts of his administration’s legislative achievements but remains defensive about the circumstances surrounding his unsuccessful re-election campaign.

The book’s commercial performance is particularly noteworthy because Biden’s promotional activities have been limited by his health challenges.

The former president disclosed in July that he was receiving treatment for prostate cancer, explaining that his doctors remained encouraged by his response to treatment. More recently, he indicated that his condition had affected his ability to participate in as many promotional interviews and public discussions as originally planned.

Despite those limitations, the reported bestseller achievement demonstrates that Biden’s political legacy continues to attract considerable public interest, even after his departure from the White House.

The success also gives the former president an opportunity to communicate directly with readers, defend his record and present his interpretation of the decisions that defined his administration.

For Biden, Promise Me, America is therefore more than a presidential memoir; it is an attempt to preserve his political legacy, explain his leadership philosophy and remind Americans of the democratic principles and economic opportunities he believes should define their country.

His message of appreciation ultimately places the achievement in the hands of readers, whom he credits for transforming his personal account of presidential leadership into a bestselling publication.

news.title: Essence Festival bids farewell to New Orleans after 30 years
news.text:
The Essence Festival of Culture, a fixture in New Orleans that has celebrated Black American culture for more than 30 years, is leaving the Big Easy.

Festival organisers and Essence Communications, which founded the annual event, announced Tuesday across their social media platforms that Essence Fest will relocate next year. The statement did not give a reason for the decision or mention where the festival was moving to. It mostly expressed gratitude to the city and its residents for helping grow the event over the years.

“You didn’t simply host us. You embraced us,” the statement said. “And in doing so, you helped shape one of the most beautiful celebrations of Black culture in the world.”

The multiday festival takes place around the Fourth of July weekend and draws major musical acts. Usher, Megan Thee Stallion and Janet Jackson are among the many performers who have headlined in recent years.

On the same day of the Essence announcement, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno teased that on December 9 the city will announce details about a new “world-class” festival dedicated to black American culture.

“Ultimately, we are working to team up with some of this country’s top black producers to essentially bring in a festival that 1) realises how important it is to be in the city of New Orleans and that the city of New Orleans itself is a draw,” Moreno said in a social media video. “We need to make sure that there’s widespread benefit for our local businesses, particularly our local black businesses.”

The Essence Festival was launched in 1995 as the Essence Music Festival when Essence magazine staged a concert event in New Orleans to mark the publication’s 25th anniversary. The magazine was acquired by Time Inc. in the early 2000s before becoming black-owned again in 2018 when the founder of Sundial Brands purchased it. It’s part of Essence Communications, a media company that includes digital and video content.

The festival has also become a political draw with panels focused on politics and voter mobilisation. Politicians, both black and white, who are in the middle of big campaigns have made Essence Fest a stop. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris spoke there in 2024 during the presidential campaign.

The Rev. Al Sharpton, founder and president of National Action Network, has participated in every festival since it began in 1995. The civil rights leader said he was saddened that such a cultural institution was leaving New Orleans but pledged continued support.

“My commitment to ESSENCE is not contingent on its geography,” Sharpton said in a statement Wednesday. “Wherever the Festival lands, I will be there.”

According to a report Essence released earlier this month, the festival generated US$1.3 billion in economic impact from 2022 through 2025. It also supported 11,000 jobs and led to $179.3 million in tax revenue.

However, local businesses and residents have questioned how much the festival benefits the community. During the festival, a “Clean Zone” ordinance prohibits smaller events in certain areas unless they are authorised.

A legal dispute arose in 2023 when a black-owned bookstore and coffee shop sought to host an event promoting black authors during the festival. The business and Essence organisers later resolved the dispute.

A similar incident occurred in 2022 when Spotify and a New Orleans real estate developer wanted to put on an event at a music club. Essence dropped the lawsuit the following year, according to NOLA.com.

news.title: Indian American leaders share Thanksgiving messages
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 27 (IANS) Indian American Congresswoman-elect Pia Dandiya recalled the Indian dishes she once resented at her family’s Thanksgiving table, saying they now symbolise what she values about America, as community leaders marked the holiday with messages of gratitude, service and belonging. Dandiya, elected to represent Florida’s 22nd Congressional District, wrote on Thursday that her childhood Thanksgiving meals combined turkey and traditional accompaniments with Indian side dishes. “I used to resent the sneaking in of Indian dishes into this meal, but now it represents the best of Thanksgiving to me,” she wrote on her campaign account. For Dandiya, the combination represented the freedom to take pride in both her family’s origins and its future in the United States. “My parents believed in it when they came here, and I believe in it today,” she wrote, adding that she was grateful for the opportunity to serve her home state. Other leaders focused on people facing hardship during a holiday associated with family gatherings and shared meals. California Congressman Ami Bera urged people to remember households struggling to afford food, heating and housing. “My hope is that we show kindness, look after one another, and come together as a country,” he wrote. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani spoke of tables with too little food, empty seats left by missing loved ones and neighbors uncertain whether they would have a safe place to eat. “May this Thanksgiving remind us not only of what we have, but of what we're capable of changing together,” he wrote. California Congressman Ro Khanna thanked his community for the opportunity to serve, while Illinois Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi encouraged people to appreciate loved ones and help those in need. Washington Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal expressed gratitude for representing her district and wished people “joy, a good meal, and rest.” Michigan Congressman Shri Thanedar thanked his family and loved ones and expressed appreciation for the opportunity to serve in Congress. Virginia Congressman Suhas Subramanyam shared a family photograph with his greeting. Arizona Congressman-elect Amish Shah, elected from the state’s 1st District, said he was grateful to call Arizona home and wished people a meaningful celebration with loved ones. Maryland Lieutenant Governor Aruna Miller thanked families, neighbors, volunteers and public servants who support others throughout the year. Virginia Lieutenant Governor Ghazala Hashmi offered a message for people grieving during the holiday. “For those missing loved ones around the Thanksgiving table, may this day land gently & with comforting memories,” she wrote. FBI Director Kash Patel thanked bureau personnel, law enforcement partners, first responders and military members spending Thanksgiving away from their families. He also acknowledged the families supporting those on duty. Second Lady Usha Vance reposted Vice President JD Vance’s Thanksgiving greeting. The vice president separately said their family had served lunch to troops at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio on Wednesday, an event also documented by the White House. “It's always important, especially today, to give thanks for those who serve our great nation,” he wrote. Former assistant attorney general for civil rights Harmeet K. Dhillon described Thanksgiving as her favorite holiday. She wrote about spending it with her mother and her mother’s two dogs, with a North Carolina pecan pie among the dishes. Former Vice President Kamala Harris shared a video about Thanksgiving cooking and hosting, including her signature dish and her husband’s onion goggles. The Indian Embassy in Washington posted a Thanksgiving greeting, while diaspora organization Indiaspora thanked its members, partners, contributors, volunteers and staff. Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai offered a lighter contribution on Thanksgiving Eve, sharing a dessert-stacking game called One More Pie and challenging players to beat his high score.

news.title: Democratic kingmaker who chose Biden AND Kamala champions new 2028 prospect… but White House buzz sparks panic
news.text:
Despite being a former Vice President, Joe Biden was trailing his Democratic rival Bernie Sanders to be the party's next candidate for president in early 2020.

Enter the kingmaker.

On February 26 of that year, longtime South Carolina Congressman Jim Clyburn – often referred to as the godfather of the state's Democratic politics – threw his weight behind Biden, giving him the seal of approval among the crucial Black vote.

'South Carolina should be voting for Joe Biden,' said Clyburn, who has been in office since 1993 and was then the House majority whip.

Biden would go on to trounce Sanders and win the Democratic primary in the Palmetto State, before sweeping 46 contests in total and winning the nomination.

The rest, of course, is history.

Biden and Clyburn remained close through his presidency.

And when it all came crashing down after that disaster TV debate with Donald Trump in June 2024, Clyburn was one of the last people to speak to Biden over the phone as he deliberated whether to step aside and who to endorse as his replacement.

Clyburn urged Biden to back Kamala Harris. 

Now, still two years out from the 2028 election and perhaps emboldened by the Democratic midterm 'bluenami' takeover of Congress, it appears Clyburn, 86, is heaping praise on another Democrat with eyes for the White House: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

'She is a very gifted politician,' Clyburn told the Daily Mail in an exclusive interview. 'If she were to run for any office, she would be a very formidable candidate.'

A long breakfast with the 37-year-old socialist New York Congresswoman in Washington some months ago left him liking AOC 'a lot,' he explained.

During Harris's ill-fated 2024 run, Clyburn memorably described her as 'my girl.'

Asked whether he'd now give AOC the same designation, he said with a chuckle: 'Yeah, I got a lot of girls. I got three daughters.'

But other Democrats in South Carolina are less taken by the prospect of having a contender from the party's far-left wing, known as 'The Squad,' on the ticket.

A key South Carolina Democratic operative, who spoke to the Daily Mail anonymously, praised AOC as an 'attractive, articulate candidate' but warned: 'Running for president in South Carolina would be a waste of her time and money. Her positions are, even for Democrats, too far left.' 

South Carolina is a traditionally deep red state, though Democrats made inroads in the midterms this year with Annie Andrews flipping Darline Graham's Senate seat blue for the first time since 1998.

The state is crucial to Democratic presidential hopefuls as it holds the party's first primary race.

The anonymous insider suggested that AOC would be better off putting any White House dreams on ice and instead mount a challenge against an increasingly unpopular Chuck Schumer.

The Democratic Senate leader is facing growing dissatisfaction among the party's liberal base, who want to harness the resounding midterm wins with a tougher challenger to President Trump.

Nationally, polling shows AOC falling in the top tier of potential Democratic presidential candidates alongside former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and even Harris.

Despite that, former South Carolina Governor Jim Hodges, who led the state from 1999 to 2003, said it is 'unlikely that a left-wing candidate' or anyone 'associated with the Democratic Socialists of America' could win the state's primary.

While this month's midterms signaled a shift to the benefit of 'younger, new candidates,' there are other contenders in the race who 'better reflect the views in Orangeburg County,' a heavily black, rural stronghold in Clyburn's district, Hodges explained.

In other words, AOC is too metropolitan, too liberal, too radical. 

Jim Messina, Obama's 2012 campaign manager and former deputy chief of staff, told the Daily Mail: 'South Carolina is an interesting combination of African American voters and moderate to conservative Democrats.

'To win that, you're gonna have to build a coalition from those two things.'

For her part, AOC has so far played coy about any 2028 plans.

Asked on Fox News about a potential White House bid two weeks after the midterms, she said: 'I think, right now, this election just happened. We got to work on getting results for people.'

She recently filed paperwork with the Federal Election Commission to run for New York's 14th Congressional district in 2028, setting up a bid for a sixth term in the House.

But that's a routine step which leaves options open.

Her fans aren't waiting. New York City's DSA chapter recently voted to urge her to run for president.

But at the same time, even some of her natural allies remain unsure.

Behind closed doors, ultra-liberal NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani recently admitted that he is still not sure whether she will run, Axios has reported.

At a press conference earlier this month, however, Mamdani said AOC 'would make an amazing whatever it is she wants to run for.'

Ocasio-Cortez's team did not respond to the Daily Mail's request for comment.

Sign up for DC Insider – the Mail newsletter that has Washington talking
news.summary: Despite being a former Vice President, Joe Biden was trailing his Democratic rival Bernie Sanders to be the party's next candidate for president in early 2020. Enter the kingmaker.

news.title: Trump’s 'manosphere' gamble backfires spectacularly with young men
news.text:
Donald Trump’s flirtation with podcasters and other online personalities was a big part of the success he had with young men in the 2024 election cycle. A lot of them came over to the GOP. Two years later, they’ve made a major swing in the opposite direction.

Exit polling from the New York Times shows that men between the ages of 18 and 29 favored Democrats 62 to 35 percent in this month’s midterm elections, according to an analysis by the Boston Globe’s Opinion section. That’s a major flip from the 55 percent to 41 percent favoring Trump over Kamala Harris that they expressed in 2024. The Globe says this shift is one of the largest recorded among any voting bloc. Young women backed Democrats at about a 4-to-1 clip.

It’s a sore spot because the president made a huge play for the “manosphere.” Not only did Trump do an interview with streamer Adin Ross, who gave the president a Rolex and a custom-wrapped Cybertruck, but Joe Rogan endorsed the president on the eve of the 2024 election. In her memoir, “107 Days,” Harris linked her defeats among young men under 30 to people in the manosphere like Andrew Tate and Myron Gaines.

It seems that a lot of the president’s base among young men has turned against him. Clayton Rasche, 25, of New Orleans, told the Globe that many of the young men who listened to those podcasts eventually felt like the president “was bought.” Rasche said he voted in 2024 to end wars, cut costs, bring transparency and fight corruption. He credits Trump with the One Big Beautiful Bill but said most of his other promises fell flat. Some of his favorite podcasters have said the same thing, the Times reported on Nov. 14.

Young men are worried about the economy. A poll from the center-left think tank Third Way showed that the top issues among young men before the election were the cost of living, jobs and corruption. About two in three men under 50 fear they will not be able to afford a home, retire or build wealth.

But the shift in support may also have had more to do with who actually showed up to vote than who switched their vote. Charlie Sabgir, the director of the Young Men Research Project, found in pre-election surveys that young men who supported Harris in 2024 were more likely to vote this year than the young men who voted for Trump. Many young men who didn’t go to college or who live in rural areas simply didn’t show up to the polls, Sabgir said. Harris voters also outnumbered Trump voters at the polls on Nov. 3, according to exit polls from NBC.

Dan Cassino of the Fairleigh Dickinson University Poll said that Democrats’ focus on equity for minorities and LGBTQ people could turn off young white men who still value traditional ideas of masculinity. But Richard Reeves of the American Institute of Boys and Men said that men aren’t necessarily looking for a party that’s just for them.

The GOP has taken note. Vice President JD Vance posted a mea culpa on X after election night, which is a sign, says the Globe, that the GOP is already worried about young men heading into the 2028 election cycle.

news.title: A Federal Judge Blocks the FCC's Review of ABC's Licenses, Saying It Likely Violates the First Amendment
news.text:
A federal judge on Wednesday ordered a halt to an unprecedented early review of the broadcast licenses held by ABC-owned stations, saying it posed an "existential threat" that was apt to have a chilling effect on the TV network's constitutionallly protected editorial decisions. Loren AliKhan, a Joe Biden appointee on the U.S. District for the District of Columbia, issued a preliminary injunction after concluding that ABC is likely to prevail in its claim that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) violated the First Amendment by retaliating against the stations for speech that offended President Donald Trump and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.

"Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face—loss of their broadcast licenses—the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness," AliKhan writes. "No one doubts that the Commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit. But in doing so, Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech."

AliKhan "saw the FCC's attempts to punish ABC for what they are: a campaign of intimidation and retaliation against speech that displeases Donald Trump," Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in an emailed press release. "The First Amendment does not allow government officials to appoint themselves the journalism or comedy police. The Constitution recognizes that even good-faith government actors cannot adjudicate journalistic merits without letting political agendas cloud their judgment, and Brendan Carr is far from a good-faith actor."

Last April, the FCC announced that it was reviewing the licenses of all eight TV stations owned by ABC: WABC in New York, KABC in Los Angeles, WLS in Chicago, WPVI in Philadelphia, KTRK in Houston, KGO in San Francisco, WTVD in Durham, North Carolina, and KFSN in Fresno, California. That announcement came years before the licenses ordinarily would be up for review. The FCC had not invoked its early-review authority in more than half a century, and it had never before simultaneously reviewed all the licenses held by one network's company-owned stations.

The official justification for the FCC investigation was the concern that Disney, which owns ABC, had violated the agency's "equal employment opportunity regulations" by engaging in discrimination under the banner of "diversity, equity, and inclusion" (DEI). But Carr made it clear that the review would also consider the broader question of whether ABC's stations were complying with their vague statutory obligation to operate in "the public interest"—a standard he thinks precludes programming decisions that he deems biased against the president.

The context of the license review showed that Carr's concerns extended far beyond the "invidious forms of DEI discrimination" he perceived. For nearly a decade, Trump has been threatening to revoke broadcast licenses in response to news coverage he views as unfair and unbalanced, frequently complaining about ABC specifically.

On September 11, 2024, the day after Trump's presidential debate with Democratic nominee Kamala Harris, which was moderated by ABC News, he complained that it was "a rigged deal" and condemned ABC as "the most dishonest news organization," adding that "they ought to take away [ABC's] license for the way" it had conducted the debate. The month after the debate, Trump reiterated that "ABC should lose its license" because of "what they've done." Shortly after taking office as the FCC's Trump-appointed chairman, Carr reopened an investigation of the charge that ABC's fact checking during the debate qualified as "broadcast news distortion"—a claim the agency had previously deemed groundless.

"ABC & NBC FAKE NEWS" are "two of the worst and most biased networks in history" because they "give me 97% BAD STORIES," Trump complained on Truth Social in August 2025. "THEY ARE SIMPLY AN ARM OF THE DEMOCRAT PARTY AND SHOULD, ACCORDING TO MANY, HAVE THEIR LICENSES REVOKED BY THE FCC. I would be totally in favor of that because they are so biased and untruthful, an actual threat to our Democracy!!!"

Trump reiterated that threat an hour later. ABC and NBC are "two of the absolute
worst and most biased networks anywhere in the World," and they "should lose their Licenses for their unfair coverage of Republicans and/or Conservatives," he said. "Crooked 'journalism' should not be rewarded, it should be terminated!!!"

The following month, late-night comedian Jimmy Kimmel delivered a monologue on his ABC talk show in which he erroneously suggested that conservative activist Charlie Kirk's assassin was a Trump supporter. Two days later, Carr publicly threatened ABC stations with fines or license revocation if they failed to punish Kimmel for his ill-informed but constitutionally protected remarks. ABC and its affiliates immediately fell in line by suspending Kimmel's show for a week—the punishment that Carr had recommended.

Trump was unsatisfied by that outcome. "I can't believe ABC Fake News gave Jimmy Kimmel his job back," he said. "I think we're going to test ABC out on this."

The FCC "should look into the license of NBC, which shows almost exclusively positive Democrat content," Trump wrote on Truth Social in October 2025. "Likewise, ABC Fake News—About the same thing, 97% negative to Republicans!"

At a press conference that November, Trump re-upped his complaint. "I think the license should be taken away from ABC because your news is so fake and it's so wrong," he told Mary Bruce, the network's chief White House correspondent. "And we have a great commissioner, the chairman, who should look at that because I think when you come in and when you're 97 percent negative to Trump, and then Trump wins the election in a landslide, that means obviously your news is not credible and you're not credible as a reporter."

The next day, the White House issued a press release, headlined "ABC 'News' Is Fake News," averring that "ABC 'News' is not journalism—it's a Democrat spin operation masquerading as a broadcast network." The White House said "the network's longstanding commitment to hoaxes, character assassinations, and outright fiction targeting only one side of the political aisle is a deliberate deception to wage war on President Trump and the millions of Americans who elected him to multiple terms."

Trump followed that up with another Truth Social post four days later. "ABC & NBC, in particular, are a disaster—A VIRTUAL ARM OF THE DEMOCRAT PARTY," he said. "They should be viewed as an illegal campaign [of] the Radical Left. NO EXPANSION OF THE FAKE NEWS NETWORKS. If anything, make them SMALLER!"

Trump revisited that theme in December. "If Network NEWSCASTS, and their Late
Night Shows, are almost 100% Negative to President Donald J. Trump, MAGA, and the
Republican Party, shouldn't their very valuable Broadcast Licenses be terminated?" he wrote. "I say, YES!"

A month later, the FCC launched an investigation of the ABC talk show The View, casting doubt on its longstanding exemption from the agency's "equal time" rule, without which interviews with political candidates would be legally perilous. "For years," Carr complained on X in January, "legacy TV networks assumed that their late night & daytime talk shows qualify as 'bona fide news' programs—even when motivated by purely partisan political purposes. Today, the FCC reminded them of their obligation to provide all candidates with equal opportunities."

Trump had frequently criticized The View, and Carr shared his antipathy to the show. "Once President Trump has exposed these media gatekeepers and smashed this facade, there's a lot of consequences," Carr remarked in July 2025. "I think the consequences of that aren't quite finished. And look, The View's got a lot of challenges there."

Last April, Kimmel offended the president again, this time by making a joke alluding to Trump's age and his wife's feelings about their marriage. Trump condemned that "really shocking" bit on Truth Social, saying, "Jimmy Kimmel should be immediately fired by Disney and ABC." The FCC announced its early review of ABC licenses the very next day.

In July, ABC and NBC declined to air a primetime speech by Trump. Those decisions were unremarkable given a long line of similar judgment calls by TV networks under administrations of both parties. But Trump was outraged.

"NBC and ABC fake news have both said that they would not cover this speech," Trump said during the address, which included dubious claims about election fraud. "They knew what it was about" but decided not to broadcast it "because of the fact that they don't like the topic, because they know how corrupt our system is and they don't want to reveal it," he averred. "They and others in the media are part of a plot." He added that "fraud like this should mean a revocation of their licenses."

Carr lent support to that suggestion at a press conference the following week. "When you have the president of the United States standing inside the White House delivering an important speech, I think that's something that broadcasters should be carrying," he said. He added that "Disney's decision there" would be one of the "points raised" during the ABC license review.

"The decision by broadcasters to carry or not carry the speech is something that is likely to be raised by petitioners that are seeking to have the FCC not renew the license for the Disney ABC stations," Carr explained in a subsequent interview. "We are looking into this question itself about the decision to air programming or not."

Carr, in short, seems to share Trump's understanding of ABC's "public interest" obligations, which the president thinks the network has violated by fact-checking him, covering him in a way he does not like, declining to give him the attention he thinks he deserves, and airing speech that irks him, including criticism and jokes at his expense. In light of Trump's anti-ABC rants and the FCC chairman's evident agreement with his beef, it is not surprising that AliKhan saw merit in the network's argument that the commission's threat to put its stations out of business was motivated by a desire to punish conduct protected by the First Amendment. That history reveals the ABC proceedings as part of Trump's broader attempt to weaponize the FCC against his opponents.

The ABC license review is "more intrusive, burdensome and extreme than anything I observed as a chairman," Mark Fowler, who chaired the FCC during the Reagan administration, said in a declaration supporting the network's lawsuit. "The blatant interplay between presidential complaints respecting ABC's broadcast content and subsequent [FCC] punitive actions," he added, "define[s] the Chairman as a biased political operative with a personal stake and bias in this case's outcome. Never in its history has the agency ever acted so corruptly and unlawfully to intrude on broadcasters' First Amendment rights."

The threat of license revocation, AliKhan notes, already has had an impact on ABC's programming decisions. In response to Carr's "equal time" investigation, ABC said, it "must now evaluate any invitation to a political candidate for its potential consequences, including whether it might later be cited by the Commission as a basis for non-renewal in the Stations' impending license renewal proceedings." The View's producers started avoiding interviews with political candidates and even began eschewing clips of politicians that might provoke FCC scrutiny. Kimmel's show likewise decided not to air an interview with James Talarico, then a U.S. Senate candidate, which was instead shown on YouTube.

"The impact of the FCC's censorship spree has not been limited to ABC or other outlets Carr has pursued directly," Stern said. "He has put broadcasters on notice that if their coverage provokes a Truth Social tantrum, the FCC may deem hurting the president's feelings contrary to the 'public interest' and come after them with bogus investigations. Outlets that Carr has intimidated can breathe a little easier. The lesson to learn from this ruling is don't cave to Carr or any other anti-speech bullies in this administration. Instead, take them to court—the judiciary is on to them, and they lose regularly."
news.summary: The FCC "may not retaliate against or punish" broadcasters "for disfavored speech," U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan says.

Things were looking rather bleak on Monday, according to several media outlets, for the presidential ambitions of California Gavin Newsom. An example of the downbeat attitude towards Newsom's political future came via the UK Daily Mail with this depressing assessment: "Gavin Newsom's 2028 dream in tatters as Senator Jon Ossoff vaults to top of crowded Democratic field."

Of course that upbeat attitude towards Jon Ossoff, at the expense of Newsom, is doomed to change once the Democrat rank and file discover that Ossoff is on record for supporting the funding of Israeli defense systems including the Iron Dome. He sat down with Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres at the international climate conference in Turkey before traveling to Poland and finally Lviv to visit wounded Ukrainian soldiers.Back stateside, he stopped in Washington for wildfire aid talks, rolled out an AI safety plan and made sure to be photographed with presumptive Speaker Hakeem Jeffries and the five new California House Democrats his redistricting push helped elect. (He also took advantage of the Capitol’s swarm of cameras and ready-made presidential backdrop to take a few headline-bait swipes at President Donald Trump.)“You got the leader of the free world who says it’s not my responsibility, he’s abdicated any leadership on this and responsibility — it’s deeply alarming,” Newsom told Playbook on the Hill about Trump’s response to recent tech and infrastructure outages.

news.title: Nobody Believes in Kamala Harris
news.text:
Her message, her record, and her word salads apparently had nothing to do with it. She also holds the distinction of being the first female vice president and the first vice president of color, and that's a story Democrats eat up. There's a theory that the party is too invested in identity politics to deny the nomination to the first minority woman vice president, and let’s be honest, that theory holds up, and it spells a huge problem for the Democrat Party.

That said, it's clear the establishment doesn't want to nominate the woman who spent over a billion dollars in 2024 to lose every single swing state… to Donald Trump. From where I sit, it’s obvious nobody outside of Kamala and her inner circle truly believes in her, and that includes the man who made her political career.

Willie Brown, the 92-year-old former San Francisco mayor, wants her to stay out of the race.

"I'm sorry that she even thinks about running for president. I don't want her to run," Brown said.

Brown argued that Kamala already made history as the highest-ranking elected woman in the country, and he suggested she could move on to a second career running a major institution or working in media.

Asked how she handled her 2024 loss to President Donald Trump, he didn't sugarcoat it. "She was clearly very hurt," Brown said.

Why does this matter? Well, Brown knows Kamala about as well as anyone in California politics, because he's the one who opened the doors for her in the first place. The two dated in the mid-1990s, when Kamala was a 29-year-old prosecutor and Brown was the 60-year-old speaker of the California Assembly, who was also married at the time.

That’s right, Kamala, we won’t forget that.

While they were together, Brown handed her appointments to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board and the California Medical Assistance Commission, and he later helped her capture her first elected office as San Francisco district attorney in 2003. When the guy who built your résumé says he's sorry you're even thinking about running, you might want to listen.

ICYMI: Mitch McConnell’s Final Power Play Could Put the Kibosh on a Trump Nominee

Brown has doubted her ability to connect with voters before, once saying she lacked a "Baptist preacher flavor in her soul.” Of course, other factors may be at play. He also has another protégé in the 2028 mix: California Gov. Gavin Newsom. Brown made his career too, putting Newsom on San Francisco's Parking and Traffic Commission, helping him land a seat on the Board of Supervisors, and backing his winning run for mayor in 2003.

Brown clearly sees Newsom as having a better chance of winning.

In a June interview with ABC News, Brown called Kamala the "most recent loser" before turning to the 2028 field.

"When you embrace somebody for the job, you really want to embrace a winner," he said. "And Newsom would be what you would have to say at the moment is a winner."

Brown clearly picked his favorite.

For Kamala to get such a verdict from Brown is devastating. In the end, everyone, even people on the left, sees Kamala for what she is: a terrible candidate who isn't very bright and who lost big to Trump.
