news.title: Chuck Schumer Odds of Defeat by Van Hollen as Ruffalo Issues Call to Action
news.text: Mark Ruffalo told his fans to call their senators and press them to elect Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen as Senate majority leader, a day after about 35 celebrities and Democratic donors signed a letter backing Van Hollen over New York Senator Chuck Schumer. The outside campaign comes five days before Senate Democrats pick their leader by secret ballot on December 1. Polling shows Democratic voters, and in particular people who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, prefer Van Hollen by wide margins. Van Hollen's supporters are testing whether phone calls and a letter bearing famous names can sway a vote senators cast in private. Yet prediction markets give Schumer more than a 90 percent chance of keeping his job, and public whip counts still favor him. Newsweek has reached out to the offices of Schumer and Van Hollen for comment via email. Mark Ruffalo Says Senators Are 'Listening' Ruffalo, who has pushed Democrats from the left for years, posted the video on X with the caption: "Chuck Schumer has a lower public approval rating than Trump. Read that again." He directed viewers to a call-in line, 877-219-6902, that connects them with Senate offices. "As of right now, the majority of Democratic senators are undecided, and they're listening to what their constituents are saying," Ruffalo said in the video. "And with Chuck Schumer having a lower public approval rating at this moment than [President Donald] Trump does, there is a very good chance that we can vote for a new leader." Ruffalo cast the December 1 vote as the first real test for the new majority, with senators choosing "whether to yet again vote for Chuck Schumer for Majority Leader, a status quo Democrat, or Chris Van Hollen, who will fight for the values and policies" voters backed in the midterms. The actor first endorsed Van Hollen in an Instagram post earlier this month. Ruffalo did not cite a specific poll in the video. But post-election surveys partly back up his argument. An Economist/YouGov poll of 1,623 U.S. adult citizens, conducted November 20 to 23, found 40 percent of Democrats would rather have Van Hollen lead the party in the Senate, compared with 19 percent who chose Schumer. Among 2024 Harris voters the gap grew to 48 percent to 18 percent, according to figures reported by Common Dreams. The poll's margin of error is about 2.9 percentage points. Democratic voters had soured on Schumer well before Van Hollen entered the race. A Politico poll in June found that 47 percent of likely Democratic voters thought Schumer should step down from leadership, while 28 percent said he should stay. More recently, a Pew Research Center survey conducted November 9 to 15 found that 49 percent of Americans viewed Schumer unfavorably, compared with 22 percent who viewed him favorably. Among Democrats, 40 percent viewed him unfavorably and 33 percent favorably. Who Signed the Letter The letter, first reported by The New York Times, was released Tuesday. Its signers include actors Jane Fonda, Robert De Niro, Marisa Tomei and Morgan Spector, comedian Chelsea Handler, television host Padma Lakshmi, Veep creator David Mandel, playwright V, formerly known as Eve Ensler, and former BlackRock executive Morris Pearl. Producers Bruce Cohen and Laurie David and documentary filmmakers Fisher Stevens and Amy Ziering also signed. The group, based mostly in Los Angeles and New York, says it donated or helped raise about $23 million for Democratic House and Senate candidates this cycle. "The Democratic Party has a trust and credibility problem, and fixing it requires Senate leaders willing to challenge the entrenched interests and power structures that protect those in power, in both parties," the letter reads. The signers want every senator who caucuses with Democrats to back Van Hollen in public, and they tied that request to how the vote is run. The leader "will be chosen behind closed doors, by secret ballot," the letter says. De Niro said in a statement that "Americans voted for the change necessary to fight the corruption, cruelty and policies of Trump and his Epstein-class cronies." "This is a window," Handler told the Times. "We need to, like, get the ball and run with it. And I don't believe that Chuck Schumer is going to do that." Progressive groups and unions have piled on. MoveOn, Indivisible, Our Revolution, the Working Families Party and the Democratic Socialists of America back the challenge, as do the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers and National Nurses United. "Accountability starts at the top. That's why we're organizing to elect Chris Van Hollen as Senate Democratic leader," Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of the progressive group Our Revolution, told Newsweek. "We need a leader who's willing to name that pressure and stand up to it." Change.org petitions calling for a new leader passed 100,000 signatures a day after they launched. Chuck Schumer's Defenders Point to the 2026 Midterm Wins But for some strategists, Schumer has already earned another term. Democrats took back the Senate on his watch, flipping seats few in the party expected to win a year ago. Jim Kessler, co-founder of the center-left think tank Third Way, said Schumer's plan for winning the Senate rested on driving Trump's approval below 40 percent, making affordability the top message and keeping unelectable candidates from winning primaries in key states. "Even Schumer's harshest critics within the party believe he deserves credit for that," Kessler told Newsweek. Several of the senators backing Schumer have made the same argument. "Under Leader Schumer, Democrats won at least 55 seats. He earned his position as Majority Leader next Congress, and together we'll deliver for Wisconsin families," Wisconsin Senator Tammy Baldwin said. Nevada Senator Jacky Rosen said Schumer "did the work to deliver what will soon be a 56-seat Senate majority against all odds." "Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible," said Maine Senator Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats. What Prediction Markets Say On Kalshi, the market on who will be Senate majority leader in the 120th Congress gave Schumer a 91 percent chance on Thursday. Van Hollen was at 9 percent and Hawaii Senator Brian Schatz at 2 percent, with about $6.5 million traded. Polymarket's "Next Senate Majority Leader?" market had nearly the same numbers, with Schumer at 92 percent, Van Hollen at 7 percent and Schatz at 1 percent, on about $1.9 million in volume. His price has mostly gone up this month. On Election Day, before anyone had announced a challenge, Kalshi gave him a 79 percent chance of winning the post and Van Hollen 4 percent. By November 10 his chances had reached 89 percent. They slipped to 86 percent after Van Hollen launched his bid on November 12, then climbed back. Can Outside Pressure Move a Secret Ballot? The winner needs a simple majority of the caucus, or 28 votes if all 55 Democratic senators and senators-elect cast ballots. Public commitments still favor Schumer. As of Sunday, at least 16 Democrats had endorsed him, compared with six for Van Hollen. An unofficial whip count published by Drop Site had 16 senators committed to or leaning toward Schumer and nine toward Van Hollen. A Washington Post tally found 30 of the 55 had said nothing publicly. Van Hollen's public backers include Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, Oregon Senator Jeff Merkley, Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin and Senators-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan. "This isn't about being against Chuck Schumer," El-Sayed said in a statement shared with reporters on Saturday. "I'm grateful for his partnership over the past few months of our general election campaign. This is about meeting the demands of the moment." Several other incoming Democrats, among them Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Troy Jackson of Maine, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire and Juliana Stratton of Illinois, have said they won't support Schumer but haven't committed to Van Hollen. Van Hollen said on November 22 that he has support from "north of 15" senators. Schumer's allies expect him to get more than 40 votes. Schumer keeps saying the race is over. "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," he wrote on X the night Van Hollen entered. Asked about the challenge last week, he told reporters, "We are united together on lowering costs and ending corruption." "Well, I'm the underdog, but we are really moving in the right direction here," Van Hollen said on NPR's Morning Edition. He has also announced he will skip a possible 2028 presidential run to focus on the leadership race, and he has played down Schumer's role in the midterm wins. "This was not a Washington-orchestrated election around the country," he said on ABC's This Week. Senators are not required to say how they voted. The caucus meets Monday. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Actor Mark Ruffalo and 35 stars are pushing senators to dump Chuck Schumer for Chris Van Hollen.

news.text:
Nairobi Senator Ediwn SIfuna with Kenyan-born photographer Polly Irungu in the USA. [LMM,X]

Kenyan-born photographer Polly Irungu, a former White House photographer who worked with former US Vice President Kamala Harris, has joined Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna’s US Diaspora Tour as the official photographer.
Irungu is volunteering her time and expertise to document the tour, describing her involvement as a personal contribution to the Linda Mwananchi campaign.
She previously served as a photographer and photo editor for former Vice President Harris and currently works as a photographer for Maryland Governor Wes Moore.

Beyond her work in government, Irungu is the founder of Black Women Photographers, a global network bringing together more than 2,100 photographers from over 60 countries.
The organisation seeks to connect Black women photographers with mentorship, professional opportunities, and networks to advance their careers in the photography industry.
Her involvement adds an international creative dimension to Sifuna’s diaspora engagements, which are part of the Linda Mwananchi campaign.

news.title: Kelsey Grammer calls American Dream a ‘gift’ he wants to pass down to his 8 children
news.text: Kelsey Grammer believes the American Dream is alive and well, and the "Frasier" star is determined to make sure his eight children understand the freedom and opportunity that come with it. During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 71-year-old actor reflected on the values he hopes to instill in his children as the United States of America celebrates its 250th anniversary, and he helps commemorate the nation's history through the collector's book "The America Opus." "The thing I most want to pass down to them is the understanding that it's your job. Your gift is the American dream," Grammer said. "What it entails is up to you." KELSEY GRAMMER WARNS OF CHILLING DANGER FACING AMERICANS WHO FORGET NATION'S FOUNDING HISTORY "Every individual has the same right to figure out what that dream is and to make it happen," he added. The "Cheers" alum shared his view that the American Dream is not just about achieving personal success, but also about having the opportunity to make a difference. WATCH: KELSEY GRAMMER ON WHAT HE WANTS HIS 8 CHILDREN TO LEARN: 'YOUR GIFT IS THE AMERICAN DREAM' Grammer pointed to Alexander Graham Bell as an example of someone who made his American Dream a reality while helping others, noting that the inventor's efforts to help deaf children communicate eventually led to the development of the telephone. "My hat is off to people who end up thinking of something that millions of people need. Why wouldn't we allow those people success? Why wouldn't we praise them? Sort of laud them as being the examples of how wonderful America is," Grammer said. "These people are all American heroes by virtue of the fact that they kept working at their dream," he continued. "Their dream was to help somebody. And it ended up helping millions of people." When asked how he hopes his children will remember him beyond his Hollywood career, Grammer emphasized the importance of setting an example through hard work and personal responsibility. THE FOUNDING FATHERS GAVE US AMERICA. 250 YEARS LATER, WE STILL DEPEND ON GOOD DADS "I hope they look on me as a guy who was incredibly fair. Firm. I have high expectations of people, I expect people to show up," he said. "Because I do. One of my sayings that I say to people is like, if I've got a job being done around the house and I haven't seen the guys for a few weeks, I say, 'You know, if I did my job this way, I wouldn't have this house, I wouldn't have anything else." "You gotta show up," Grammer continued. "That's the big thing. Your American dream actually is in your hands. I mean, and I do say this to a lot of people these days, I say like, 'Anybody tells you the American dream's over, don't give them your vote because that's what they want. They want it over. Theirs is that it's over. You know, no thanks." Grammer, who has been married four times, shares his eldest child, daughter Spencer Grammer, 43, with his first wife, Doreen Alderman. He is also father to daughter Greer Grammer, 34, whom he shares with his ex-girlfriend Barrie Buckner. The "Grand Isle" actor has daughter Mason Olivia, 25, and son Jude Gordon, 22, with his ex-wife Camille Grammer, 54. He married British former flight attendant Kayte Walsh in 2011. Grammer and Walsh are parents to daughter Faith Evangeline, 14 and sons Kelsey Gabriel, 12, Auden James, 10, and Christopher, 1. 'MELROSE PLACE' STAR ANDREW SHUE SAYS 70% BELIEVE THE AMERICAN DREAM IS 'DEAD OR DYING' While speaking with Fox News Digital, Grammer, who previously indicated that he has considered running for office, said that for now, he had set aside his political ambitions to focus on fatherhood. "I have put it on the back burner because I've got all these new kids and I really want to be a present dad," he said. Grammer admitted that he has regrets over not being present enough for his older children earlier in their lives. WATCH: KELSEY GRAMMER REFLECTS ON 250 YEARS OF U.S. HISTORY IN NEW BOOK 'AMERICA OPUS' "My first couple of kids — I wasn't around for them as much as I would have liked to have been," he said. "And I think they may even still have some sensibilities about that, sensitivity about it, rather, and I'd like to make it up to everybody because you need a dad there." Grammer went to say that he didn't have an understanding of what fatherhood meant after growing up without his own dad. The actor's parents, Frank Allen Grammer Jr. and Sally Cranmer Grammer, divorced when he was two years old, and he was raised primarily by his mother and maternal grandparents. In 1968, Grammer's father was shot and killed in the U.S. Virgin Islands when the actor was just 13. "I didn't have a dad, you know, I didn't know what it was to be called a dad till I was one," he said. "I'd never used the word till I became a dad. So it's really important to me, but a good dad, hopefully, would be what you want in office. You want a guy that shows up." Grammer also explained how he believes he has changed after becoming a father again later in life. "I've got four kids with my current wife, Kate, and it's such an extraordinary experience," he said. "It's just that — it's so lovely in every way. These surprising young human beings that are in your life and in your care, and you're gonna do your best to not mess them up, but we always do." "Kind of not really — I mean, look, I'm steady," he continued. "I'm a steady guy. Maybe I wasn't always, but I am now, and I'm proud of that and that they have that to look to." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS The six-time Emmy Award-winner went on to share the biggest lesson that he had learned about love and marriage after more than 15 years with Walsh. "Just stay in it," he said. "You just stay, you know, stay, work it out. I mean, Kate's a particularly level-headed woman." PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE "I always think of that song, Cat Stevens' song, 'I'm looking for a hard-headed woman,'" Grammer continued. "One that will make me do my best. She's the kind of person you want to do your best for. And so I'm here." Grammer recently teamed up with British luxury publisher Opus to create "The America Opus," a large-format illustrated book celebrating the United States' 250th anniversary. "The America Opus" explores pivotal moments in American history, highlighting the people, achievements and challenges that have shaped the country over the past two and a half centuries. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE The book features historical photographs, imagery and stories documenting America's legacy, including both its triumphs and challenges. "The America Opus" will be released in two editions, including the Marquee Edition, which is limited to 2,500 copies at $2,500, and a smaller Classic Edition with fewer pages. "What's nice about the book is we're not actually out to — we have no axe to grind or no political stance to make," Grammer said. "We're actually basically just doing some snapshots of extraordinary moments in the American story." "Some of them when we were in the ascendancy. Some of them maybe not our best story, not our best foot forward, but you know what, we're pretty open and honest about all that," Grammer continued. "But there's no reflection other than the fact that this has been an extraordinary experiment, the American experiment," he added. "And the 250 years that we've lived will hopefully point to another 250 that are just as extraordinary." "The America Opus," which is available for preorder and is expected to begin shipping in December, features an introduction by Grammer and a foreword by President Donald Trump, who also signed it. "I've never known a guy who loves America more than him," Grammer said of Trump. "But I will say this, if Kamala Harris had been the president when we were doing this book, we would have asked her to write a forward and sign it because it's about the sitting president of the United States during the 250th birthday." "Not necessarily because they wanted to, but because they were in a place where they could. It's like the land of the possible, that's why I always think of America. And so this points to that."

news.title: 2026's biggest political turkeys: Scandals, gaffes and other memorable unfortunate moments from this year
news.text: As 2026 comes to a close, several political blunders, missteps, and serious allegations have left prominent politicians and notable figures presumably looking back with regret. Here are the top political turkeys who made headlines for unfortunate reasons this year. Eric Swalwell Heading into 2026, Eric Swalwell was a well-known member of Congress and the leading Democratic contender in the race for governor of California. By March, he had become the frontrunner in the race and looked poised to take control of the nation’s largest economy in a state where Democrats rarely lose in statewide general elections. Shortly after, that all changed when allegations of sexual assault and other misconduct surfaced in April, prompting prominent Democrats to swiftly withdraw their endorsements and call for Swalwell to abandon his gubernatorial bid. SWALWELL’S FORMER DEM RIVAL UNLOADS ON HIS ‘LIGHTWEIGHT’ CAREER AS SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS EMERGE Swalwell denied the sexual assault allegations, but within days he suspended his campaign and resigned from Congress amid bipartisan calls for his ouster, which effectively ended his political career and put him in potential legal jeopardy. Swalwell faces a federal investigation and separate probes in New York and Los Angeles into sexual assault allegations, which he denies. FBI agents seized his electronic devices and searched his Washington home in August, and in October searched a Beverly Hills mansion where he had stayed. No criminal charges have been filed. Tim Walz In 2024, Walz was elevated to the top of the national scene when he was chosen by former Vice President Kamala Harris to be her running mate for president. Since then, Walz’s political fortunes have taken a downward turn after the Harris-Walz ticket lost the presidential election, leading some pundits to criticize the decision to add him to the ticket. In January 2026, Walz’s political career took another hit when he announced he was dropping his bid for re-election as governor amid a massive fraud scandal that is estimated to have cost the state billions. Polling in June showed that Walz’s approval rating had dropped to its lowest level since he took office. ANGER SWELLS AFTER SWALWELL'S 'OPEN SECRET' WITH WOMEN WENT UNREPORTED FOR YEARS Republicans in Congress Republicans faced historical headwinds heading into the midterm elections and were dealing with significant voter frustration on issues like gas prices and affordability. While many expected Democrats to have a good night on Nov. 3, the GOP ended up losing control of both chambers of Congress ahead of President Donald Trump’s final two years in office. Additionally, Democrats picked up control of the majority of governorships in the United States as well as control of the majority of state legislatures, giving the party a dominant presence it hasn’t seen in decades. Axios reported that 75% of Americans now live in a state with a Democratic governor and 53% live in a state where Democrats control the legislature and the governorship. TIM WALZ SAYS HE TAKES RESPONSIBILITY FOR MINNESOTA FRAUD BY NOT RUNNING FOR RE-ELECTION Jasmine Crockett After years as one of the most recognizable and outspoken Democratic members of Congress, Crockett will be out of a job on Capitol Hill in 2027 after opting against House re-election to pursue an unsuccessful Senate bid. Her decision followed Texas Republicans’ redrawing of the congressional map, which reduced the number of Democratic-leaning seats in the Dallas-Fort Worth area from three to two and scrambled the plans of three Democratic incumbents. Crockett’s redrawn 30th District remained Democratic-leaning, but she chose a statewide campaign rather than seeking another House term. Crockett lost the Democratic primary to state Rep. James Talarico in March, then reignited tensions by describing the contest as a "racist race" and pushed back against expectations that she would campaign alongside him. "People keep trying to say, ‘Well, Jasmine has to go and hold his hand.’ No, I don’t," she said during a July podcast appearance, arguing that supporting Black candidates further down the ballot would help increase turnout. Although Crockett and her campaign said she had endorsed Talarico through her post-primary call to support the Democratic ticket, her reluctance to campaign with him and his omission from her political action committee’s endorsements fueled questions about her enthusiasm. Talarico defended her, saying he welcomed her endorsement, while Crockett maintained that elevating lesser-known candidates would benefit Democrats on the ballot. Talarico ultimately defeated Republican Ken Paxton by about 12 percentage points, becoming the first Texas Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat there since Lloyd Bentsen was re-elected in 1988. Francesca Hong The socialist Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate was dominating in the polls heading into the August Democratic primary, but her campaign stumbled in its final days as she struggled to explain past calls to cancel Thanksgiving before narrowly losing to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, a candidate who had exited and then returned to the race. The controversy centered on a resurfaced 2020 social media post in which Hong wrote, "Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621," and criticized celebrating colonialism. Asked on CNN in August whether she still wanted the holiday canceled, Hong initially emphasized that Thanksgiving was painful for some communities rather than directly rejecting her earlier position. She later reversed course, saying she loved Thanksgiving and did not want to cancel it. After losing the primary, Hong acknowledged that she regretted the CNN interview. Cindy Hyde-Smith The Republican senator lost her seat in deep-red Mississippi to Democrat Scott Colom after an answer about rising beef prices became damaging campaign fodder. Asked by WLOX anchor Hugh Keeton about rising beef prices during a local television interview, Hyde-Smith responded, "You know, you have so many proteins to choose from." Colom later used the exchange in a campaign ad featuring voters saying they would rather pick another senator. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Colom ultimately defeated Hyde-Smith by just 8,031 votes, a margin of less than 1 percentage point — close enough that her remark, amplified by her opponent’s advertising, could have made the difference in a race that cost Republicans a seat many believed was safe. Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich singled out the remark while discussing Republican losses with Larry Kudlow on Fox News before the race was called, arguing that suggesting cheaper food failed to address voters’ economic frustrations. "I mean, it’s not the job of a senator to explain her failure by suggesting a new diet," Gingrich said. Other honorable mentions include Democratic Fayette County Council candidate Jaime West, who was ridiculed by critics who said she appeared to be drunk and slurred her way through attacks on Republicans during a televised candidate forum; Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, whose controversial ad featuring his opponent’s mother drew fierce blowback before he lost his race; and Maine Democratic Senate candidate Graham Platner's fall from grace as he suspended his campaign after being accused of sexual assault.

news.title: Holder says 2028 Democratic presidential candidates must campaign for restoring US as a 'DEI-infused nation'
news.text: Obama-era Attorney General Eric Holder suggested that any Democrat who wants to win in 2028 needs to campaign to restore America to being a "DEI-infused nation" once again. Holder appeared on Monday’s episode of MS Now host Nicolle Wallace’s "The Best People" podcast, where they talked about how the Democratic Party should respond to the impact of the second Trump administration and chart a new course for America going forward. "What do you see in the crop of 2028 Democratic presidential candidates that gives you hope that we're not just going to get through these two years but potentially head to something better?" Wallace asked. "Because I don't think a person can be nominated as the next Democratic candidate for president who won't say, ‘What has happened before is unacceptable. This is my plan to get us back to, you know, a DEI-infused nation. We're going to confront our history. We're going to make our political system more fair. We're going to hold accountable to the extent that we can people who did inappropriate things in the prior four years,’" he said. DEMOCRATS SIZE UP 2028 IN DENVER. WE ASKED WHO’S READY TO RUN He added, "I don't think a Democratic candidate can win the nomination without saying those things and then actually hope for re-election without doing those kinds of things and I think the American people are looking for fighters." Wallace went on to agree that voters have been seeking such leaders for years, caring less about how far left they are. "This is the piece that I feel like the media still gets wrong as well. People have said, ‘Aren't you worried about how left some Democrats are?’ And my audience, that I'm not sure that I understand all their politics, what they are drawn to like almost 100% of the time is the people fighting," she said. Earlier in the interview, Holder criticized the rhetoric of "’Make America Great Again’" and asked, "When did you think America was great? I mean, really? Is it like the ‘Leave it to Beaver’ years when June Cleaver was vacuuming with pearls?" He added, "That was a time when, you know, Black folks were segregated, women were relegated then to household work, people in the LGBT community were in the closet. That's when you think America was great. No, America's great in its present form, or greater." KAMALA HARRIS URGES DEMS TO 'BE RUTHLESS' WITH POWER AFTER MIDTERMS, DEMANDS TRUMP ACCOUNTABILITY He then checked himself, noting that America may not be so great under Trump’s leadership, but said even now, it is ultimately better than it was in past eras. He added that those who appeal to America’s past "look back to an America that is kind of mythical, but never really existed, that's what they're really trying to do here. And I think we have to, every now and again, pull back and try to see the big picture of what these folks are trying to do. And that is chief among the reasons why we have to oppose them, and we use the political system to do it." White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster talked to Fox News Digital: "President Trump was resoundingly elected with a mandate to end divisive, racist policies and restore merit and efficiency. DEI ran rampant during the Biden Administration, and Americans ultimately paid the price for these destructive policies with a restricted labor pool, higher operational costs, and workforce inefficiencies. The Trump Administration will always promote equal treatment under the law for every American, regardless of race or ethnicity." Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy during Trump's first term, spoke to Fox News Digital about the exchange, arguing this is the Democratic Party revealing its true agenda after winning the midterms on affordability. "This is right on cue. Democrats ran on affordability and anti-corruption, but that was a ruse to convince voters," he said. "Once they are in office, the goal is to 'infuse' the country with DEI because their real goal is a radical revolution that overturns and replaces our historic institutions and enshrines a race-based policy that caters to their favorite interest groups and voting blocs. This is what Democrats really believe, and anyone who thinks 'woke' is dead is either a liar or a fool." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

news.title: Joe Biden's Memoir Is Full of Easily Disproven Lies
news.text:
Joe Biden has a long, well-documented record of fabricating and exaggerating his own biography, and he keeps repeating debunked stories as if saying them often enough could make them true.

For example, his son, Beau Biden, died of brain cancer at Walter Reed in 2015, yet Joe has repeatedly claimed that Beau "lost his life in Iraq."

And then there's another whopper he loves to tell about having an "epiphany" as a teenager that turned him into a champion of gay rights.

According to Biden, during his senior year of high school, his father dropped him off in Wilmington when they saw two men in suits kiss. "Joey, it's simple. They love each other,” Biden claims his dad told him. He calls that moment the "epiphany" that shaped his views on same-sex marriage.

His actual record shows no such epiphany ever happened.

As a senator, Biden opposed letting gay people work in the federal government because he considered them a security risk. He backed "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" and voted for the Defense of Marriage Act, and even as vice president, he initially opposed civil unions for same-sex couples.

When a man spends decades lying about his past to build a political brand, it's inevitable that his presidential memoir will be full of whoppers too.

Sure enough, a Washington Free Beacon review by Jon Levine found that Promise Me, America is loaded with factual errors and embellishments.

The biggest one involves Biden's first Senate run.

In the book, Biden wrote that he was "angered by a growing pattern of lies coming out of Washington" when he ran in 1972, and he named Richard Nixon's Watergate cover-up as one reason. The problem is the chronology doesn’t support this fairy tale. The Watergate break-in happened on June 17, 1972, months after Biden had launched his Delaware Senate campaign.

Biden, then 29, formally declared his candidacy in January 1972, but he was already calling himself a "candidate" in 1971, and a November 1970 profile pegged him as a Democrat hopeful for the 1972 race. The scandal didn't unravel until the spring of 1973, and by then Biden had already won and taken the oath of office.

ICYMI: Mitch McConnell’s Final Power Play Could Put the Kibosh on a Trump Nominee

According to the Free Beacon, its line-by-line analysis turned up enough mistakes to suggest nobody ever fact-checked the book. And I’m sure that was intentional. A review in the U.K. Observer said the book is "rather obviously written by committee," produced by the same former West Wing operation that scripted Biden's presidency.

I don't think anyone actually believes Joe Biden wrote this book. I'm sure a bunch of people worked with him and his ghostwriter to bring it all together, but clearly, Biden's insistence on putting narratives before facts remains.

Take the American Rescue Plan Act. Biden wrote that the bill cleared the Senate on March 7 with Vice President Kamala Harris casting the tie-breaking vote, which he called "the first in a record number" of her tiebreakers.

However, the Senate actually passed it on March 6, 2021, by a 50-49 margin. So final passage did not need a tiebreaker. In fact, Kamala had already cast her first tie-breaking vote back in February 2021.

What a stupid thing to get wrong. And for what?

The border section is worse, since immigration is the issue that helped send Donald Trump back to the White House.

In the memoir, Biden called the February 2024 border deal "the toughest, most effective immigration and border bill ever put together," and he wrote that it would shut down the border if "more than four thousand people a week" tried to enter.

Not true. The actual bill would have triggered a shutdown at 5,000 crossings per day, or about 35,000 per week. Biden's version inflates the bill's toughness on an issue about which he faced bipartisan criticism for inaction.

The Free Beacon also found at least a dozen misstated dates and smaller errors. Biden placed his 2020 campaign kickoff rally in Philadelphia in April 2019, for example, even though it happened in May 2019, a date the book's own endnotes get right. Sloppy. Sloppy. Sloppy.

Telling lies about your story on the campaign trail or in an interview is bad enough. But people expect a stronger commitment to accuracy in a book. We’re not talking about spinning a story in a positive way; we’re talking about blatant factual errors and outright lies. That lack of interest in the truth in his presidential memoir, his final attempt to shape his presidential legacy, is a reflection of the dishonesty he’s demonstrated throughout his career.

news.title: Women Have Always Shaped America
news.text:
American women flexed their political muscles in the 2026 election, participating as voters and candidates, influencing outcomes, and breaking records by sending more women than ever to hold statewide elected office. Several states elected female governors for the first time. Women aren’t a monolithic voting bloc, but they are a powerful force in American politics. 

This has been true since the beginning. Our country would not be what it is today without the contributions of countless women — some of whom are widely recognized in history books, but many of whom are not. This Thanksgiving holiday, we should reflect on all the freedoms and privileges we have as American women and the debt of gratitude we owe to those who came before us.

During the American Revolution, women organized boycotts of British goods, raised money for the cause, supplied soldiers in encampments, and worked as cooks, laundresses, and nurses alongside the men. Some women even acted as spies. Elizabeth Burgin, a mother of three, helped more than 200 American prisoners of war escape from the British. Women like Margaret Corbin and Mary Ludwig Hays (also known as "Molly Pitcher") even loaded and fired field cannons after their husbands fell in battle.

Throughout the 19th century, women shaped our young country. Although their direct political influence was limited, the importance of their indirect influence cannot be overstated. For example, Dolley Madison transformed the office of the First Lady into a proactive role and used her position to bring people together. She may be remembered most for hosting parties, but the result of her efforts was greater bipartisanship. 

In the 1830s, Alexis de Tocqueville toured America and made observations about our democracy, comparing and contrasting it to Europe. He had a lot to say about American women, and essentially credited them with the success of our vibrant civil society. He wrote: “I have nowhere seen woman occupying a loftier position; and if I were asked…to what the singular prosperity and growing strength of that people ought mainly to be attributed, I should reply: To the superiority of their women.”

Around this same time, a woman named Sarah Josepha Hale was a writer and editor for ladies’ magazines. By today’s standards, she might not be considered a feminist because she strongly believed that women’s primary sphere was domestic life, but she advocated for new opportunities for women, including in higher education. Before and during the Civil War, she petitioned five different American presidents, asking them to establish the national holiday of Thanksgiving. Like Dolley Madison, she understood that there was power in bringing people together around a table.

Later in the 19th century, Harriet Tubman would lead dozens of slaves to freedom on the Underground Railroad. Other women, like Sojourner Truth, Lucretia Mott, and Sarah and Angelina Grimké, and many others were leaders in the movement to abolish slavery. 

Many people know the suffrage movement of the early 20th century resulted in the 19th Amendment, guaranteeing women the right to vote nationwide in 1920 (thanks to women like Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton). But some don’t know that Wyoming was the first place to recognize women’s suffrage, in 1869 while it was still just a territory. The state of Montana became the first state to elect a woman to Congress, Rep. Jeannette Rankin, in 1916.

In the 1940s and throughout World War II, women’s roles evolved to meet the needs of a nation at war. “Rosie the Riveter” became symbolic of women who took on traditionally masculine roles. They welded ships, built tanks, assembled bombs, operated heavy machinery, and worked as scientists, code breakers, and engineers in the war effort. In the private sector, millions of women entered the workforce during this time, keeping the economy going while the troops were fighting abroad. 

The latter part of the 20th century and the first part of the 21st century have seen enormous progress, and countless glass ceilings have shattered. Women like Ella Baker and Rosa Parks made invaluable contributions to the civil rights movement of the 1960s. Sandra Day O’Connor became the first female supreme court justice in 1981. Sally Ride became the first American woman to go to outer space in 1983. Kamala Harris became the first female vice president of the United States in 2021. 

All along, we’ve had political debates about the status of women and the roles we should play. While many women achieve greatness in their professions, many more make contributions to their families, neighborhoods, and communities through consistent acts of service and love. We may not always “have it all” if that means having the perfect work-life balance. But we do have the freedom to make choices, to participate as citizens, and to pursue happiness as we see fit. 

America should be proud of its women. And American women should be proud of our country. This Thanksgiving, I’m thankful for the women who’ve come before me, and I’m committed to serving my country, as they did, and paying it forward to those who’ll come after me. 

Hadley Heath Manning is a senior fellow at Independent Women.

news.title: Ben & Jerry’s Is Super Thankful for the Violence of Abortion
news.text:
What does ice cream have to do with abortion?

Absolutely nothing. But that never stopped Ben & Jerry’s founders, Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield, from churning milk into frothy abortion activism. You name the far-left cause, they were on the bandwagon. Perhaps they were even driving it. What’s fascinating to me is how two white Jewish men think that abortion needs to happen more in black communities where abortion is already the number one killer of black lives. Which flavor would that be, anyway? Genocide with Chunks of Racism? 

Of course, Ben & Jerry’s calls it “Reproductive Justice.” Civil rights icon Fannie Lou Hamer called it “genocide.” Jesse Jackson (before he ran for president on the Democrat ticket) called it “genocide.” Dr. Alveda King, niece of Dr. Martin Luther King, calls it “crime against humanity” and “racist.” What is just about disproportionately killing the most marginalized black lives?

Ben & Jerry’s declared their fake war on white supremacy in 2024 (ironically the very thing that past and present abortion workers accuse Planned Parenthood of): “…the culture of white supremacy must be dismantled to achieve equity for all marginalized people. We have focused our strategies on outcomes for Black people because slavery and its legacy remain such a defining element of American life.”

Abortion is one of slavery’s sordid legacies. Dr. Mildred Jefferson, the first black woman to graduate from Harvard Medical School (and first female surgeon at Boston Medical), explained this: “I would guess that the abortionists have done more to get rid of generations and cripple others than all of the years of slavery and lynchings.”

Ben & Jerry’s apparently thinks limitless abortion should always be on the menu, as it declares on its website: “Roe was always meant to be the floor — not the ceiling — for abortion rights.”

Empower Mint

In the company’s relatively new podcast, Into the Mix, it heavily pushes abortion propaganda disguising it as liberation and empowerment. The episode, entitled “Liberating Abortion,” features Ashley C. Ford, a self-described lesbian and New York Times bestselling author, as well as abortion activist Renee Bracey Sherman. The entire podcast centers on disinformation and the importance of “abortion storytelling.” Sherman repeatedly describes the failure of telling good emotional stories, while her own storytelling is painfully bland and filled with meaningless word salads.

In true Kamala Harris style, Sherman unleashes a tirade of words at war with one another to sum up her worldview at the start of the podcast: “It’s truly at the core of my views on abortion and making sure that everyone has access to safe and healthy pregnancy care but also my view of the world in that every child, every baby, every mama, every parent, every trans person, everyone deserves the healthcare that is most affirming to them and that they get it when they need it.”

She never once mentioned prenatal care in the podcast. Virtually zero Planned Parenthoods offer it (it’s less than 0.1 percent of its services). Being dismembered, sucked out with an aspiration machine, or snuffed out with a DIY chemical abortion pill is not affirming for any child.

The gist of Sherman’s story is that she had a crappy boyfriend that she regularly had sex with during her early years in college. She was 19, allegedly worked at Victoria’s Secret, and didn’t have enough money to get (low-cost, often no-cost) birth control pills. There were numerous contradictions in her story. In the podcast version, she claimed the abortion cost $450. In her 2016 op-ed in Women’s Health magazine, it was $350. She also told the host that she only had a credit card with a max of $500, yet she somehow paid for the $450 abortion and the $100 “twilight sedation” charge on that same card? Somehow, her math ain’t mathin’.

In the podcast, she claimed she sat alone in the abortion mill and wished she had someone there supporting her. She never mentioned, as she did in the op-ed, that her boyfriend took her there and, though he initially wanted them to choose adoption, he backed her abortion decision — until they arrived there. The Ben & Jerry’s remix of this part is typical of “abortion storyselling.” They demonized anyone who opposes abortion, falsely smeared pregnancy centers who help millions, and ignored the fact that loving the post-abortive doesn’t mean affirming the violence done to them.

Sherman boasted in both the podcast and her op-ed about how “progressive” her parents were and accepting of abortion. In the article, she proclaimed: “Abortion was never out of the question. I grew up in a politically progressive family where it was a sin to not vote or not have an opinion on an issue…While we may not have talked about abortion in a very in-depth way, I knew from a young age that our family stood with Planned Parenthood and that my mother felt abortion was a reasonable option.” Then why was it hard to go to them?

At one point in the same article, she mentioned that her boyfriend would have “sex with her while she was asleep.” Um. Normally, people would call this rape. Bizarrely, it didn’t deserve such recognition from Sherman.

One Sweet Whirled

“I wasn’t ready to parent. And to be honest, I simply didn’t want to be pregnant.” Sherman’s story — true or not — sadly, is not unique. My wife, Bethany, understands the same feelings of not being ready to parent. In her 20s, she found herself in a toxic relationship, walked away, and within weeks found out that she was pregnant. The economics weren’t right. The guy wasn’t right. The timing wasn’t right. But killing her unborn child wasn’t right regardless of the circumstances. Bethany rejected the violence of abortion.

Ben & Jerry’s wants us to believe that the world is sweeter when we kill our offspring. Every one of its flavors is tainted with the bitter taste of abortion extremism. I scream, you scream, we (should) all scream for life-affirming ice cream.

news.title: Thanksgrifting
news.text:
The losers who don’t know how to give thanks.

Mossad folks tend to keep their mouths shut — that’s part of their business. My wife’s cousin used to point out where their office is while saying that it was forbidden to point out where their office was. So it was a bit of a surprise when former Mossad chief David Barnea casually mentioned that it was his outfit that prevented an ISIS attack at a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna. According to his explanation, the Austrians provided raw intelligence which the Mossad “processed” and helped to bring an end to the plot and the arrest of the terrorists. This is a beautiful example of how things are supposed to work. Unfortunately, Israel is one big one-way street, both when I drive around here and in the world at large.

After the announcement that Israel helped prevent a repeat of the Manchester Arena bombing, I would have expected Taylor Swift to put out a statement thanking the Mossad for its efforts to keep her fans safe. And maybe she made a private call to Binyamin Netanyahu and offered five discs as her form of thanks. But thanks from lefties are rare. They feel totally entitled, and anything done for them was deserved, earned, and expected. Swift is wealthy, talented, and also smart. She knows that if she were to thank Israel, she would anger her mostly lefty fan base. What is it worth saying thanks if the paying customers will stop buying her music and merchandise? Remember when she threw her support to Kamala Harris? How did a reelected Donald Trump repay her? He congratulated her on the announcement of her engagement to football star Travis Kelce. Trump is in another league compared to the ingrates on the left.

Thanksgiving was always beloved — lots of family, food, and football. A long weekend and then...shopping. I was in the open market “shuk” recently and saw a big turkey at one of the local butchers. It was waiting for its American patron to buy it. “Jews” are called in Hebrew, “Yehudim”, from the name of the fourth son of Jacob, Yehuda. The root of this name is “Hoda’a” which means thanks. Not far from my house is Rechov (street in Hebrew) George Washington. At the end of it, you will find Rechov Abraham Lincoln. Not far outside of Jerusalem, one can find a quiet, pastoral place in the John F. Kennedy Forest. The first street one hits when arriving in Tel Aviv has always been Laguardia. There are three 9/11 memorials in Israel — and not because of the Israelis or even the Jews who were killed on that day. It is a testament to the bond that Israel feels for America and the American people. news.title: After 3 decades, Essence Music Festival bidding farewell to New Orleans
news.text:
NEW ORLEANS (AP) — The Essence Festival of Culture, a fixture in New Orleans that has celebrated Black American culture for more than 30 years, is leaving the Big Easy.

Festival organizers and Essence Communications, which founded the annual event, announced Tuesday across their social media platforms that Essence Fest will relocate next year. The statement did not give a reason for the decision or mention where the festival was moving to. It mostly expressed gratitude to the city and its residents for helping grow the event over the years.

“You didn’t simply host us. You embraced us,” the statement said. “And in doing so, you helped shape one of the most beautiful celebrations of Black culture in the world.”

The multiday festival takes place around the Fourth of July weekend and draws major musical acts. Usher, Megan Thee Stallion and Janet Jackson are among the many performers who have headlined in recent years.

On the same day of the Essence announcement, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno teased that on Dec. 9 the city will announce details about a new “world-class” festival dedicated to Black American culture.

“Ultimately, we are working to team up with some of this country’s top Black producers to essentially bring in a festival that 1) realizes how important it is to be in the city of New Orleans and that the city of New Orleans itself is a draw,” Moreno said in a social media video. “We need to make sure that there’s widespread benefit for our local businesses, particularly our local Black businesses.”

The Essence Festival was launched in 1995 as the Essence Music Festival when Essence magazine staged a concert event in New Orleans to mark the publication’s 25th anniversary. The magazine was acquired by Time Inc. in the early 2000s before becoming Black-owned again in 2018 when the founder of Sundial Brands purchased it. It’s part of Essence Communications, a media company that includes digital and video content.

The festival has also become a political draw with panels focused on politics and voter mobilization. Politicians, both Black and white, who are in the middle of big campaigns have made Essence Fest a stop. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris spoke there in 2024 during the presidential campaign.

The Rev. Al Sharpton, founder and president of National Action Network, has participated in every festival since it began in 1995. The civil rights leader said he was saddened that such a cultural institution was leaving New Orleans but pledged continued support.

“My commitment to ESSENCE is not contingent on its geography,” Sharpton said in a statement Wednesday. “Wherever the Festival lands, I will be there.”

According to a report Essence released earlier this month, the festival generated $1.3 billion in economic impact from 2022 through 2025. It also supported 11,000 jobs and led to $179.3 million in tax revenue.

However, local businesses and residents have questioned how much the festival benefits the community. During the festival, a “Clean Zone” ordinance prohibits smaller events in certain areas unless they are authorized.

A legal dispute arose in 2023 when a Black-owned bookstore and coffee shop sought to host an event promoting Black authors during the festival. The business and Essence organizers later resolved the dispute.

A similar incident occurred in 2022 when Spotify and a New Orleans real estate developer wanted to put on an event at a music club. Essence dropped the lawsuit the following year, according to NOLA.com.

news.title: For Trump, doubling down on tariffs is about power, not popularity
news.text:
PALM BEACH - In midterm elections three weeks ago, US voters punished Republicans over an economy and inflation that many said were made worse by tariffs. President Donald Trump is doubling down on them anyway.

The Trump administration on Nov 25 announced a new round of tariffs on goods from 14 major trading ​partners, including China, Japan and the European Union, a seemingly counterintuitive move that reflects both Trump’s decades-old belief in tariffs and a new political reality confronting his White House.

With Democrats set to control Congress for the final two years of his presidency, tariffs are taking on added importance as one of the most potent economic tools Trump can wield without lawmakers’ approval.

Tariffs are taxes levied on imports, raising costs for consumers. But Trump sees them as a way to wring concessions from foreign leaders, force corporate CEOs to build plants in the US, raise cash for the government and curry favour with blue-collar voters, according to US officials and other people familiar with the president’s thinking.

And after a midterm defeat for his party that threatens to sharply constrain his domestic agenda, Trump is eager to demonstrate that he remains capable of driving economic policy and exercising power even as his legislative clout diminishes, the people said.

“This is all because of tariffs,” Trump told CNBC on Nov 23 as he touted new factories being built in the US. But he said the policy could come with costs. “There’s going to be always that little headache during this little transition period.”

Some Republicans in Congress were quick to blame the president’s tariff policy for the party’s stunning midterm losses. Two-thirds of voters said Trump’s tariff policies hurt the national economy, compared with 21% who said they had helped and 12% who found no difference, according to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets. Yale University’s Budget Lab estimated earlier in November that tariffs raised US household costs by US$900 (S$1,161) annually.

The administration nevertheless proposed new tariffs that would increase duties on targeted imports, with maximum rates of 20% to 40%, though completed or pending trade deals would generally limit them to 10% to 20%.

The new policy, which followed an eight-month review of trading partners’ practices, revamps a set of tariffs that Trump imposed in 2025 and the Supreme Court struck down as illegal in February.

Trump’s chief trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, made the tariff announcement with little fanfare on the eve of the US Thanksgiving holiday. Trump himself made no public remarks on the new actions, a marked contrast with his “Liberation Day” tariff announcement in 2025 in the White House Rose Garden.

Despite the muted rollout, the market reaction was swift, with the benchmark S&P 500 closing down a quarter of a percentage point on Nov 25.

Trump had also roiled the markets just days earlier with his extraordinary efforts to restore Jensen Huang as CEO of the chipmaker Nvidia, a surprise move that tested the bounds of presidential intervention in private markets. Stock markets rallied on Huang’s return, but have since pared back.

Concerns about affordability

Democrats seized on the tariff announcement, saying Trump was willfully ignoring voters’ anger about high costs and inflation, which have also been fueled by Trump’s decision to attack Iran, sparking a conflict that has significantly disrupted oil production and shipping. Several Democrats also argued that, by punishing allies, the policy did little to thwart China’s aggressive trade practices.

“Republicans have learned nothing,” incoming House Majority Leader Katherine Clark, a Massachusetts Democrat, said on X.

A former senior US trade official who served under Trump said the midterm rout likely moderated the tariff rates proposed, given that stiffer rates could trigger fresh concerns over affordability.

But while the election focused heavily on rising fuel prices and the cost of living, Trump has made reducing the US trade deficit a cornerstone of his administration, arguing that Washington was effectively shipping factory jobs overseas.

“Putting a stop to American workers, farmers, and businesses being ripped off by lopsided trade agreements has been a key foundation of President Trump’s Make America Great Again movement,” said White House spokesman Matthew Middleton, adding that the administration would “continue fighting to lower costs”.

Tariffs also have brought a new revenue source to the federal government after Trump’s signature 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act cemented lower individual tax rates.

Trump’s protectionist policies have drawn support from some blue-collar labor groups that historically backed Democrats, even as some Republicans recoil from an economic tool they view as hostile to free markets.

United Steelworkers International President Roxanne Brown on Wednesday called the administration’s actions “long overdue”. The group endorsed Trump’s Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris, in 2024.

Republican US Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska, a Trump critic who is retiring from Congress, took a different view. Calling tariffs “a tax on American consumers” and blaming high inflation and lower wage growth for Republicans’ losses, he urged lawmakers to reclaim authority over import duties. REUTERS

news.title: Gavin Newsom to Face Uphill Battle in Possible 2028 Run, Top Democrat Strategist Predicts — as Cali Gov. Will Have to 'Overcome' Major 'Problem'
news.text:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville warned that California Gov. Gavin Newsom could face a significant obstacle if he seeks the presidency in 2028, arguing that voters may be reluctant to support a candidate so closely associated with the state's liberal politics, RadarOnline.com has learned.

During an episode of the Politics War Room podcast with political adviser Mark McKinnon, Carville acknowledged Newsom's advantages before questioning whether his home state's political reputation could undermine a national campaign.James Carville Sends Warning to Gavin Newsom"His strength is he runs the biggest state. He's got a huge fundraising base. There's no doubt about it," Carville said. "His problem is, 'Are we going to do this California s--- again? Really? Is that what we're going to do?'"

Carville said Newsom would need to address concerns about his political identity.

"He's got to overcome that kind of barrier," Carville warned, arguing that an "uber coastal candidate" might not appeal to voters looking for a different direction.Gavin Newsom's Political SkillsDespite those concerns, both strategists acknowledged Newsom's political abilities.

McKinnon said he once considered Newsom "a little too slick, a little too Hollywood," but came away impressed by his ability to communicate and defend his positions.

"I mean, he's got chops," McKinnon said. Carville agreed that Newsom possesses considerable political experience.

"To his credit, he's a real California guy," Carville said. "He don't try to fake it."Gavin Newsom's Political IdentityDemocratic strategist Doug Schoen raised separate concerns about Newsom's consistency, telling Fox News that the governor has struggled to establish a clear national political identity.

"Gavin Newsom has no clear identity," Schoen said. "His strengths are that he's telegenic, quick on his feet and engaging."

Newsom has defended his administration's record, saying California had delivered policies Democrats support across a range of issues.

California has expanded paid sick leave, provided universal free school meals and enacted abortion protections under Newsom, while critics have pointed to the state's high housing costs, taxes and homelessness problems.Gavin Newsom Sets January TimelineNewsom recently provided a timeline for deciding whether to enter the 2028 race. On November 12, the governor said he planned to discuss the decision with his family before leaving office in January.

"We'll spend the next few weeks with the family and make a decision early January," Newsom said.

The governor has also indicated that former Vice President Kamala Harris could influence his decision. During a September interview with CNN's Jake Tapper, Newsom said, "I wouldn't run if she ran."

His term as California governor ends in January 2027, when Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra takes office.

news.title: Maine Democrat Senator-Elect Troy Jackson Backs Chris Van Hollen to Oust Chuck Schumer as Majority Leader
news.text:
Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-ME), a longtime skeptic of Senate Democrat Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY), announced Wednesday that he will vote for Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) in the upcoming Senate Democrat leadership election, citing their shared support for eliminating the filibuster, passing Medicare for All, and increasing the minimum wage.

Jackson, who defeated longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) in the November midterm elections, announced his decision in a November 25 statement ahead of the December 1 secret ballot to determine who will lead Democrats’ incoming 56-seat Senate majority.

“I’ve talked with Mainers about what they need from the Senate, and I believe it’s time for a change in leadership. I’ll be voting for Senator Van Hollen. When we spoke, I told him Maine needs a seat at the table when the caucus decides what gets funded and what we’re going to fight for. I was impressed by his vision for the caucus, and I came away confident he’ll take Maine’s priorities seriously,” Jackson stated.

“From one end of Maine to the other, I heard the same thing. People are working harder, falling further behind, and getting tired of being told to wait. Senator Van Hollen and I agree that it’s time to end the filibuster, pass Medicare for All, and give working people a raise by increasing the minimum wage. I want a leader who’ll bring those fights to the floor,” he continued.

“Mainers voted for change in November, and they ought to get it. Whoever leads this caucus, I’ll fight like hell to make sure the Senate takes on the problems Mainers sent me to Washington to solve,” Jackson concluded.

Jackson’s endorsement comes as an Economist/YouGov poll conducted November 20–23 found that Democrats surveyed preferred Van Hollen over Schumer by 21 percentage points, 40 percent to 19 percent, while 2024 Kamala Harris voters surveyed favored the Maryland Democrat by 30 points, 48 percent to 18 percent. During a Sunday appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Van Hollen expressed confidence that he could secure the 28 votes needed to defeat Schumer, citing the endorsement of Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI). “We’re north of 15 and momentum is in our direction,” he said. During a November 15 appearance on ABC’s This Week, Van Hollen accused Schumer’s team of spreading “misinformation” and “trying to instill fear in people who may say that they’re going to support me as a new leader.”

Approximately 35 Hollywood figures, including Jane Fonda and Robert De Niro, have also signed a letter urging Senate Democrats to replace Schumer, according to a New York Times report covered by Breitbart News Tuesday. Comedian Jon Stewart and Marvel actor Mark Ruffalo have notably advocated a leadership change. Ruffalo subsequently faced accusations of antisemitism after calling for leadership that followed “the will of the people not entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties,” defending his remarks by citing Schumer’s 2018 AIPAC speech and calling for the consistent enforcement of domestic and international law.

Jackson, a former Maine Senate president and majority leader, defeated Collins in the November 3 election, denying the Republican a sixth term. NBC News projections showed Jackson leading Collins 52.6 percent to 47.3 percent when she reportedly called to concede. “I called Troy Jackson tonight to congratulate him and to assure him that my staff and I will work to ensure a smooth transition,” Collins stated, according to Punchbowl News senior congressional reporter Andrew Desiderio. 

Democrats backed Jackson after their initial candidate, Graham Platner, who faced scrutiny over a Nazi tattoo, exited the race following allegations of sexual misconduct and rape. Jackson’s campaign also faced scrutiny over allegations that his longtime partner is his second cousin.

Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-WV), who supported Collins’ reelection campaign, argued during an October appearance on NewsNation’s The Hill that Jackson’s decision to campaign alongside prominent progressives reflected how he would govern. “Bernie and AOC and Elizabeth, I doubt they ever knew the other opponent, Susan’s opponent, up there. And they come from the far left of the Democratic Party,” Manchin said, adding that the people a candidate chooses to campaign alongside indicate “where you’re going to go and how you’re going to vote and represent your state.”

Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-ME), a longtime skeptic of Senate Democrat Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY), announced Wednesday that he will vote for Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) in the upcoming Senate Democrat leadership election, citing their shared support for eliminating the filibuster, passing Medicare for All, and increasing the minimum wage.

news.title: Houston in talks to host Essence Fest after New Orleans departure
news.text:
The city of Houston, Texas, says it is in talks to host the Essence Festival of Culture, after festival organizers announced this week that the annual event was leaving its longtime host city of New Orleans after more than 30 years.

"With confirmation this week that the event is leaving New Orleans, we can confirm that Houston has been in direct talks with Sundial Media Group, the owner of Essence, to bring the festival to our city," Houston Mayor John Whitmire said Wednesday in a joint statement with Houston First Corporation President and CEO Michael Heckman. "Those discussions have accelerated significantly in recent weeks."

VIDEO: 2025 Essence Festival spotlights Disney, Hulu, and Nat Geo in New Orleans 

The mayor said his team is "encouraged by the possibilities" of what Essence Festival would look like if it was brought to Texas and touted Houston's "rich Black cultural heritage."

The organizers of Essence Festival, which takes places every year over the Fourth of July weekend, previously announced in a letter Tuesday that it was starting "a new chapter beyond New Orleans in 2027" and thanked festival participants and the Crescent City for its hospitality.

In a statement shared with ABC News on Wednesday, a spokesperson for Essence said in part, "We know the people of New Orleans are processing this news. After 32 years, we did not take this decision lightly, but we needed to do what was in the best interest of the community."

The spokesperson said despite the festival generating "more than $300 million in economic impact" for New Orleans, "it has to keep growing for the community it serves." 

"We have been heartened by the overwhelming interest from cities across the country to host the festival's legacy and its future," they added. "We are excited about what is ahead and committed to continuing to make ESSENCE the biggest, most joyful festival for Black culture in the world, and can't wait to share our 2027 Festival plans. To New Orleans: thank you for 32 years."

According to NOLA.com, the online news website for The Times-Picayune, the decision to part ways came after months of failed long-term contract negotiations to keep the festival in the city. The city's previous seven-year contract expired earlier this fall, according to the outlet.

Thousands have since commented on the festival's announcement on Instagram, with several people lamenting the move.

"People don't come to Essence fest just for the festivals they come for the City of New Orleans culture as well," one person commented in part. "Food, music bourbon street. It gives visitors something to do before the concerts."

Another person wrote, "If we can't go to Nola for Essence, where can you go?! It's upsetting me and my homegirls."

Following the festival's announcement, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno announced in an Instagram video that another "world-class" festival celebrating Black culture will take its place next year.

"Ultimately, we are working to team up with some of this country's top Black producers to essentially bring in a festival that one, realizes how important it is to be in the city of New Orleans, and that the city of New Orleans itself is a draw, but also one that will be able to bring in top talent to perform for you, but also to recognize the amount of talent that we have right here in the city of New Orleans with amazing musicians and artists," Moreno said.

Moreno teased another announcement, coming Dec. 9, that will provide more details and reveal what the new festival will be.

"The festival that we'll be bringing to you will also work to do activations not just in downtown New Orleans, but across the city, from New Orleans East to downtown New Orleans to Algiers," Moreno continued. "And then, of course, we need to make sure that there's widespread benefit for our local businesses, particularly our local Black businesses, when it comes to this festival. And so that's the other piece that we're building as well."

The Essence Festival has drawn celebrities, musicians, superstars and politicians to its celebrations over the years, from former Vice President Kamala Harris and former first lady Michelle Obama to Grammy-winning singer Miguel.

The 2026 Essence Festival took place this past July at the New Orleans Ernest N. Morial Convention Center and the Caesars Superdome and featured performers including Brandy, Monica, Kehlani, Latto, Cardi B., T.I., Patti LaBelle, Public Enemy, and George Clinton and Parliament-Funkadelic.

The festival concluded with an Aaliyah tribute performance curated by Missy Elliott, with performances from Mýa, Normani, Chlöe and more.

ABC News has reached out to Mayor Moreno's office for comment.
news.summary: The Essence Festival of Culture is leaving its longtime home of New Orleans after more than 30 years.

news.title: Maddow says Democrats can abolish Electoral College if they 'swing for the fences'
news.text: MS NOW host Rachel Maddow said during an interview on Saturday that getting rid of the Electoral College was "doable" for Democrats if they "swing for the fences." MS NOW's Jacob Soboroff asked Maddow about her thoughts on Democrats getting rid of the system, which has received criticism after the last two Republican presidents won their first elections despite losing the national popular vote. "My whole life, it has been this kind of theoretical, you know, this hypothetical math problem. You know, if ever enough states to speak for 270 electoral votes all got into this agreement, then it would go into effect, and it always just seems so pie in the sky," she said. GOP WIPEOUT GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE AS DEMS QUIETLY SCORE ANOTHER MAJOR WIN WITH BIG RAMIFICATIONS Maddow said she felt it was doable for the Democrats after speaking with Ben Wikler, a Democratic advocate for eliminating the Electoral College. Soboroff and Maddow said that Democrats could use the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement that makes it so a state will award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential candidate wins the overall national popular vote — regardless of who actually won the vote inside that individual state. GAVIN NEWSOM EXPRESSES 'OPENNESS' TO PACKING SCOTUS, CALLS ELECTORAL COLLEGE SYSTEM 'PERVERTED' Eighteen states have signed the compact, in addition to Washington, D.C., which means the compact has 222 electoral votes pledged to it — 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. However, Democrats now control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislatures in the swing states of Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada. Those legislatures' combined 50 electoral votes would push the compact to 272 and activate it should they vote to sign the compact. PROGRESSIVES UNVEIL $25 MINIMUM WAGE PUSH TO SOLVE AFFORDABILITY CRISIS DESPITE ECONOMIST INFLATION WARNING "There are enough Democratic states right now who have a Democratic trifecta — governor and the full legislature — that puts you way over 270 if they all decided to do it, and you don't need very many states to act right now for that to be operative," Maddow said. "It's doable. I mean, raising the minimum wage is doable. Getting rid of the Electoral College is doable, age limits for Supreme Court justices might be doable. I mean, the Democrats have big majorities and if they decide to swing for the fences, they could do a lot right now." KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS Former Vice President and 2024 Democratic nominee Kamala Harris called for major institutional changes in October during an interview, which included "changing" the Electoral College. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "I believe that we need to expand the Supreme Court. We need more justices on the Supreme Court so that we can have a court that actually reinforces the spirit and principles behind the Constitution of the United States," Harris told podcast host Keke Palmer. "I believe that we should be pushing for what is possible around changing the Electoral College. Right?" she added. Harris also lost the popular vote in 2024, making her the first Democratic White House candidate to do so in 20 years. The system allocates 538 electors to the 50 states and Washington, D.C. A majority of 270 is needed to win the presidency.
